lessons.title: Muslims After the War of Independence
lessons.notes_html:
Muslims and Hindus had jointly taken part in the War of Independence of 1857, but the British placed the entire blame on the Muslims and took revengeful action against them. As a result, the Muslims of India were devastated politically, socially and economically; their political dominance came to an end and they were reduced to the status of a defeated nation.

Their educational condition also collapsed. According to William Hunter's report, of 2,141 government recruits in 1871 only 92 were Muslims, and in 1870 only 17 of the 517 graduates of the Bombay, Madras and Calcutta universities were Muslims. The East India Company monopolised trade and destroyed local industries, and Muslim agricultural estates were confiscated on a large scale — in Bombay province alone 20,000 estates were seized.

In his pamphlet Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (1858), Sir Syed Ahmed Khan argued that the real causes of the revolt were the British government's ignorance of the conditions of its subjects and laws that did not match Indian traditions. He stressed that Hindus and Muslims had both taken part in the war, so blaming Muslims alone was unjust.

mcqs.q: Who did the British blame entirely for the War of Independence of 1857?
mcqs.why: The British placed the entire blame for the 1857 war on the Muslims and took revengeful action against them, although Hindus and Muslims had fought together.

mcqs.q: According to William Hunter's report, how many of the 2,141 government recruits in 1871 were Muslims?
mcqs.why: William Hunter's report showed that of 2,141 government recruits in 1871 only 92 were Muslims, which shows how far Muslims had fallen behind in government service.

mcqs.q: In 1870, how many of the 517 graduates of the Bombay, Madras and Calcutta universities were Muslims?
mcqs.why: Only 17 of the 517 graduates of the three universities in 1870 were Muslims, a sign of the severe educational decline of the Muslim community after 1857.

mcqs.q: How many Muslim agricultural estates were seized in Bombay province alone after 1857?
mcqs.why: Muslim agricultural estates were confiscated on a large scale after the war; in Bombay province alone 20,000 estates were seized by the British.

mcqs.q: In which pamphlet did Sir Syed Ahmed Khan explain the causes of the 1857 revolt?
mcqs.why: In Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (1858) Sir Syed argued that the revolt was caused by the government's ignorance of its subjects' conditions and laws unsuited to Indian traditions.

mcqs.q: What did Sir Syed argue about responsibility for the War of Independence?
options: Both Hindus and Muslims had participated
mcqs.why: Sir Syed emphasised that both Hindus and Muslims had participated in the war, so blaming Muslims alone for the revolt was unjust.

mcqs.q: What was the political condition of Indian Muslims after 1857?
mcqs.why: After 1857 the political dominance of the Muslims came to an end and they were reduced to the status of a defeated nation in their own country.

mcqs.q: Which body monopolised trade and destroyed local industries, according to the unit?
mcqs.why: The East India Company monopolised trade and destroyed local industries, which ruined the economic position of Indians, especially Muslims.

mcqs.q: What does William Hunter's report mainly show about the Muslims?
mcqs.why: Hunter's figures — 92 Muslims among 2,141 recruits and 17 among 517 graduates — mainly show the educational and service decline of the Muslims after 1857.

mcqs.q: In which year was Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind published?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed published Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind in 1858, a year after the War of Independence, to remove the British misconception that Muslims alone caused the revolt.

lessons.title: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and the Aligarh Movement
lessons.notes_html:
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (born 1817) believed that the only reason for the backwardness of the Muslims was the lack of modern education. He followed the principle of 'education from start to end' and wanted Muslims to acquire modern Western education, science and technology along with religious education.

His educational services

He established a school at Muradabad in 1859 where English was also taught, and another school at Ghazipur in 1863. In 1863 he founded the Scientific Society at Ghazipur to translate Western knowledge into Urdu; its office shifted to Aligarh in 1864. After visiting London in 1869 and studying Oxford and Cambridge, he launched the Aligarh Movement, set up the Committee for the Advancement of Muslims in India in 1870, established the M.A.O. High School at Aligarh in 1875 and the M.A.O. College, inaugurated by Lord Lytton on January 8, 1877. The first principal of Aligarh College was Henry George Impey Siddons.

The Aligarh Movement created a trend among Muslims to pursue modern education: the proportion of Muslims in high government positions rose and it became almost impossible for a Muslim graduate to remain unemployed. Inspired by it, institutions such as Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam and the Islamia Colleges of Lahore, Peshawar and Kolkata were established. In 1920 Aligarh College was upgraded to a university.

mcqs.q: According to Sir Syed, what was the only reason for the backwardness of the Muslims?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed believed the only reason for Muslim backwardness was the lack of modern education, so he devoted his life to spreading Western education among Muslims.

mcqs.q: Where did Sir Syed establish a school in 1859?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed established a school at Muradabad in 1859 where English was also taught; a second school followed at Ghazipur in 1863.

mcqs.q: In which year and city was the Scientific Society founded?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed founded the Scientific Society at Ghazipur in 1863 to translate Western knowledge into Urdu; its office shifted to Aligarh in 1864.

mcqs.q: What was the purpose of the Scientific Society?
options: To translate Western knowledge into Urdu
mcqs.why: The Scientific Society was founded to translate Western knowledge into Urdu so that Muslims could benefit from modern learning in their own language.

mcqs.q: In which year was the M.A.O. High School established at Aligarh?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed established the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental High School at Aligarh in 1875; it became the M.A.O. College, inaugurated on January 8, 1877.

mcqs.q: Who inaugurated the M.A.O. College in 1877?
mcqs.why: The M.A.O. College at Aligarh was inaugurated by Lord Lytton on January 8, 1877, two years after the M.A.O. High School was founded on the same campus.

mcqs.q: Who was the first principal of Aligarh College?
mcqs.why: Henry George Impey Siddons was the first principal of Aligarh College, as recorded in the book's fill-in-the-blanks exercise.

mcqs.q: In which year was Aligarh College upgraded to a university?
mcqs.why: The Aligarh Movement's crowning achievement came in 1920, when the M.A.O. College at Aligarh was upgraded to the status of a university.

mcqs.q: Which institutions were inspired by the Aligarh Movement?
mcqs.why: Inspired by Aligarh, similar institutions were established across the country, including Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam and the Islamia Colleges of Lahore, Peshawar and Kolkata.

mcqs.q: What principle of education did Sir Syed follow?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed adhered to the principle of 'education from start to end' and believed that all objectives of the Muslim community could be achieved through education.

lessons.title: Sir Syed's Political Services and the Two-Nation Theory
lessons.notes_html:
Sir Syed wanted Muslims to remain loyal to the British government, because other communities had progressed through their loyalty, and he wanted Muslims to become politically and economically stable before taking part in politics. In May 1866 he established the British Indian Association to help Indians establish relations with the British Parliament and secure their rights.

When, in 1867, extremist Hindu leaders in Banaras started a movement against the Urdu language, Sir Syed concluded that Hindus and Muslims were two separate nations and presented the Two-Nation Theory. He is therefore considered the founder of the Two-Nation Theory.

He advised Muslims to stay away from the Congress, opposed joint electorates and representative institutions in a country of many nations, and proposed separate electorates for Muslims — a proposal that later became a central demand of Muslim political leaders and a foundation for the creation of Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan is considered the founder of which theory?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed is considered the founder of the Two-Nation Theory, which he presented after concluding that Hindus and Muslims were two separate nations.

mcqs.q: Which event of 1867 convinced Sir Syed that Hindus and Muslims were two separate nations?
mcqs.why: When extremist Hindus of Banaras started a movement against Urdu in 1867, Sir Syed concluded that Hindus and Muslims were two separate nations.

mcqs.q: Why did Sir Syed want Muslims to remain loyal to the British government?
options: Other communities had progressed through loyalty
The British had promised him a title
mcqs.why: Sir Syed believed other communities had progressed through loyalty to the British, and he wanted Muslims to become politically and economically stable before entering politics.

mcqs.q: Which body did Sir Syed establish in May 1866?
mcqs.why: In May 1866 Sir Syed established the British Indian Association to help Indians establish relations with the British Parliament and secure their rights.

mcqs.q: What was the purpose of the British Indian Association?
options: To help Indians build relations with the British Parliament and secure their rights
mcqs.why: The British Indian Association was formed to connect Indians with the British Parliament so that Indian demands and rights could reach the rulers.

mcqs.q: What did Sir Syed advise Muslims about the Congress?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed advised Muslims to stay away from the Congress, because he believed its demands did not protect Muslim interests as a separate nation.

mcqs.q: Which electoral system did Sir Syed propose for Muslims?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed proposed separate electorates for Muslims, an idea that later became a central demand of Muslim leaders and a foundation for Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Why did Sir Syed oppose joint electorates?
options: India was a country of many nations, so joint electorates would submerge Muslims
mcqs.why: Sir Syed opposed joint electorates and representative institutions in a country of many nations, because Muslims would always be outvoted by the Hindu majority.

mcqs.q: Sir Syed's proposal of separate electorates later became:
options: A demand only of the Congress
A central demand of Muslim political leaders
mcqs.why: The separate-electorate proposal later became a central demand of Muslim political leaders and one of the foundations for the creation of Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Sir Syed wanted Muslims to enter politics only after becoming:
mcqs.why: Sir Syed wanted Muslims first to become politically and economically stable through education and loyalty, and only then to take part in politics.

lessons.title: The Muhammadan Educational Conference and Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam
lessons.notes_html:
In 1886 Sir Syed founded the Muhammadan Educational Conference to spread modern education among Muslims across the country. The Conference promoted Western education throughout India, encouraged the establishment of Western-style educational institutions while also ensuring religious education in them, and held annual sessions alternately in different provinces. At a time when Muslims had no political platform, it served as the only forum that brought them together: demands were presented to the government through it and plans for the promotion of education were made. It was at its 1906 Dhaka session that the Muslim leaders decided to establish the All India Muslim League.

Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam

Hassan Ali Afandi, a lawyer from Sindh, was inspired by the Aligarh Movement and established a similar institution in Sindh, supported by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Syed Amir Ali. In 1885 Lord Dufferin, the Governor-General of India, laid the foundation stone of the school building at Karachi. The institution provided both modern and religious education. Hassan Ali Afandi's son Wali Muhammad was appointed its first principal. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was a student of this institution and passed his matriculation there; it also produced leaders such as Sir Shah Nawaz Bhutto, Sir Abdullah Haroon, Sir Ghulam Hussain Hidayatullah and Ayub Khuhro.

mcqs.q: In which year was the Muhammadan Educational Conference founded?
mcqs.why: Sir Syed founded the Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1886 to spread modern education among Muslims across the whole country.

mcqs.q: What was the main purpose of the Muhammadan Educational Conference?
options: To spread Western education among Muslims
mcqs.why: The Conference promoted Western education throughout the country and encouraged Western-style institutions that also ensured religious education.

mcqs.q: Where did the Muhammadan Educational Conference hold its annual sessions?
mcqs.why: The Conference held its annual sessions alternately in different provinces, which kept Muslims of all regions connected with the educational movement.

mcqs.q: At which session of the Conference was the decision taken to establish the All India Muslim League?
mcqs.why: At the 1906 Dhaka session of the Muhammadan Educational Conference, Muslim leaders decided to establish the All India Muslim League.

mcqs.q: Who founded Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam?
mcqs.why: Hassan Ali Afandi, a lawyer from Sindh inspired by the Aligarh Movement, founded Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam with the support of Sir Syed and Syed Amir Ali.

mcqs.q: Who laid the foundation stone of Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam in 1885?
mcqs.why: Lord Dufferin, the Governor-General of India, laid the foundation stone of the school building at Karachi in 1885; the institution itself was founded by Hassan Ali Afandi.

mcqs.q: Who was the first principal of Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam?
mcqs.why: Hassan Ali Afandi's son Wali Muhammad was appointed the first principal of Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam, followed later by Percy Hyde, Thomas Henry, Wines and Harrison.

mcqs.q: Which great leader studied at Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam and passed his matriculation there?
mcqs.why: Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was a student of Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam and passed his matriculation from this institution.

mcqs.q: What kind of education did Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam provide?
mcqs.why: Like the Aligarh institutions, Sindh Madressa-tul-Islam provided both modern and religious education to its students.

mcqs.q: At a time when Muslims had no political platform, the Muhammadan Educational Conference served as:
options: The only forum that brought Muslims together
mcqs.why: The Conference served as the only forum that brought Muslims together; demands were presented to the government through it and educational plans were made.

lessons.title: Deoband and Nadwatul Ulama
lessons.notes_html:
The Deoband movement took the opposite direction to Aligarh. Its scholars considered Western education a threat to Islamic society, so Darul Uloom Deoband — established at Deoband in 1866 by Sufi Haji Abid Hussain — gave complete education in the Quran, Hadith and Tafseer, educated students with the Islamic spirit, worked to completely eliminate polytheistic customs and traditions from Islamic society, and established madrasas throughout India for the propagation of Islam. The movement refused government aid and ran Darul Uloom Deoband through its own resources. Maulana Mahmood-ul-Hasan was associated with this movement.

Nadwatul Ulama of Lucknow stood between the two. Inaugurated on September 26, 1898, it aimed to prepare students of religious schools who would be equipped with both modern and religious education, combining Eastern traditions with Western knowledge. Its proposals included a review of the outdated curriculum in religious schools, reforms in the educational system according to changing needs, and a syllabus including both religious and modern education.

mcqs.q: In which year was Darul Uloom Deoband established?
mcqs.why: Darul Uloom Deoband was established in 1866; the unit text, the timeline and the chart all date the Deoband madrasa to 1866.

mcqs.q: Who established the madrasa at Deoband?
mcqs.why: The solved book's matching exercise records that Sufi Haji Abid Hussain established the madrasa at Deoband in 1866.

mcqs.q: What was the Deoband movement's view of Western education?
options: It wanted it only for rulers
It considered it a threat to Islamic society
mcqs.why: Deoband's scholars considered Western education a threat to Islamic society, so they concentrated on complete education in the Quran, Hadith and Tafseer.

mcqs.q: Which subjects did Darul Uloom Deoband emphasise?
mcqs.why: The goals of Deoband were to give Muslims complete education in the Quran, Hadith and Tafseer and to educate students with the Islamic spirit.

mcqs.q: How did Darul Uloom Deoband finance itself?
options: It refused government aid and ran on its own resources
mcqs.why: The Deoband movement refused government aid and ran Darul Uloom Deoband through its own resources, keeping it independent of the British.

mcqs.q: One goal of the Deoband movement was to eliminate what from Islamic society?
mcqs.why: Deoband aimed to completely eliminate polytheistic customs and traditions from Islamic society and to spread Islam through madrasas across India.

mcqs.q: When was Dar-ul-Uloom Nadwat-ul-Ulama, Lucknow, inaugurated?
mcqs.why: Dar-ul-Uloom Nadwat-ul-Ulama at Lucknow was inaugurated on September 26, 1898, as recorded in the unit's solved answers.

mcqs.q: What was the aim of Nadwatul Ulama?
options: To prepare students with both modern and religious education
mcqs.why: Nadwatul Ulama aimed to prepare students equipped with both modern and religious education, combining Eastern traditions with Western knowledge.

mcqs.q: How did Nadwatul Ulama differ from both Aligarh and Deoband?
options: It worked only in Lucknow city
It accepted British aid unlike both
It stood between the two, combining Eastern tradition with Western knowledge
mcqs.why: Nadwa stood between Aligarh and Deoband: an intellectual and religious movement combining Eastern traditions with Western knowledge and a reformed curriculum.

mcqs.q: Which scholar was associated with the Deoband movement?
mcqs.why: The book's true/false exercise confirms that Maulana Mahmood-ul-Hasan was associated with the Deoband movement.

lessons.title: Formation of the Indian National Congress
lessons.notes_html:
By the late nineteenth century, Western education had produced an educated class of government employees, lawyers, teachers, doctors and businessmen who had become aware of politics and their rights, and the modern press was openly criticising government policies. A retired British officer, A. O. Hume, realised that a political party was essential through which the British government could be made aware of the demands, feelings and needs of the Indian people.

Hume consulted the Governor-General, Lord Dufferin, and with his support the All India Congress was formed in 1885. Its first meeting was held in December 1885 in Bombay, chaired by W. C. Bonnerjee, with seventy-two delegates, of whom only two were Muslims.

Objectives of the Congress

The Congress demanded that Indians be given representation in the government, that a legislative council be formed including representatives of the Indian people, that the maximum number of Indians be included in high government positions with Civil Services examinations held in India, and that representative institutions be established to pave the way for self-governance.

mcqs.q: Who took the initiative to form the Indian National Congress?
mcqs.why: A retired British officer, A. O. Hume, realised a political party was needed to convey Indian demands to the government, and he initiated the Congress.

mcqs.q: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded?
mcqs.why: The All India Congress was formed in 1885 with the support of Governor-General Lord Dufferin, whom A. O. Hume had consulted.

mcqs.q: Who presided over the first session of the Congress?
mcqs.why: The first session of the Congress was presided over by W. C. Banerjee; A. O. Hume was its founder and Lord Dufferin the Governor-General who supported its formation.

mcqs.q: Where was the first meeting of the Congress held?
mcqs.why: The first meeting of the Congress was held in December 1885 in Bombay, with seventy-two delegates attending.

mcqs.q: How many delegates attended the first Congress meeting, and how many were Muslims?
mcqs.why: Seventy-two delegates attended the first Congress meeting in Bombay, of whom only two were Muslims — an early sign of Muslim distance from the party.

mcqs.q: Which Governor-General's support did Hume obtain for forming the Congress?
mcqs.why: Hume consulted the Governor-General Lord Dufferin, and with his support the All India Congress was formed in 1885.

mcqs.q: One objective of the Congress was that Civil Services examinations should be:
mcqs.why: The Congress demanded that the maximum number of Indians be included in high government positions and that competitive Civil Services exams be held in India.

mcqs.q: The Congress wanted representative institutions established in order to pave the way for:
mcqs.why: Among the Congress objectives was the establishment of representative institutions that would pave the way for self-governance in India.

mcqs.q: What social change made the formation of a political party possible by the 1880s?
options: Western education had produced a politically aware educated class
mcqs.why: Western education had produced an educated class of lawyers, teachers, doctors and businessmen aware of politics and rights, and the press was criticising government policies.

mcqs.q: The Congress demanded a legislative council that would include:
mcqs.why: The Congress objectives included forming a legislative council including representatives of the Indian people and giving Indians representation in the government.

lessons.title: The Partition of Bengal 1905
lessons.notes_html:
The partition of Bengal took place in 1905; the new Muslim-majority province of Eastern Bengal came into existence on October 16, 1905, with its capital at Dhaka. The partition greatly benefited the Muslims: they were freed from the exploitation of Hindu traders, landlords and moneylenders, the new province provided new job opportunities, Dhaka began to flourish, the number of Muslim students increased, a Muslim press emerged and newspapers began to be published from Dhaka, and the establishment of a High Court and a university in Dhaka became a real possibility.

Why the Hindus opposed it

The first reaction came from the lawyers of Kolkata: the Calcutta Bar feared a separate High Court in the new province would transfer cases and reduce their income. Kolkata's newspapers also opposed it because newspapers would start from Dhaka and their circulation would fall. Extremist Hindus gave the partition a religious colour; Surendranath Banerjee called it a deep conspiracy against Bengali nationalism, and the Arya Samaj linked it with cow protection. Under this pressure the Congress also opposed the partition, and in its 1906 session Madan Mohan Malaviya proposed the boycott of foreign goods, launching the Swadeshi Movement. In 1911 the partition was annulled, announced by King George V at the Delhi Durbar.

mcqs.q: In which year did the partition of Bengal take place?
mcqs.why: The partition of Bengal took place in 1905, and the new province of Eastern Bengal came into existence on October 16, 1905.

mcqs.q: What was the capital of the new province of Eastern Bengal?
mcqs.why: Eastern Bengal was a Muslim-majority province with its capital at Dhaka, which began to flourish after the partition.

mcqs.q: How did the partition of Bengal benefit Muslims economically?
options: It gave them control of Calcutta
It freed them from the exploitation of Hindu traders, landlords and moneylenders
mcqs.why: The partition freed Bengal's Muslims from the exploitation of Hindu traders, landlords and moneylenders and opened new avenues of development and jobs.

mcqs.q: Which new institutions became a real possibility in Dhaka after the partition?
options: A High Court and a university
mcqs.why: With Dhaka as a provincial capital, the establishment of a High Court and a university in Dhaka became a real possibility, and a Muslim press also emerged.

mcqs.q: Why did the Calcutta Bar oppose the partition?
options: A separate High Court in the new province would transfer cases and reduce their income
mcqs.why: The lawyers of Kolkata feared that the new province would get a separate High Court, cases would be transferred there and their income would decrease.

mcqs.q: Who called the partition of Bengal a deep conspiracy against Bengali nationalism?
mcqs.why: Surendranath Banerjee called the partition a deep conspiracy against Bengali nationalism, while extremist Hindus gave it a religious colour.

mcqs.q: Which movement was launched through the boycott of foreign goods against the partition?
mcqs.why: In the 1906 Congress session Madan Mohan Malaviya proposed the boycott of foreign goods, launching the Swadeshi Movement against the partition.

mcqs.q: When was the partition of Bengal cancelled?
mcqs.why: The partition of Bengal was cancelled in 1911, announced by King George V at the Delhi Durbar in December 1911 — a severe blow to Muslim hopes.

mcqs.q: Who announced the annulment of the partition of Bengal?
options: King George V at the Delhi Durbar
mcqs.why: King George V announced the annulment of the partition at the Delhi Durbar in December 1911, under the pressure of the Hindu agitation.

mcqs.q: After the partition, the number of Muslim students in Eastern Bengal:
mcqs.why: Among the benefits of the partition listed in the book, the number of Muslim students increased and newspapers began to be published from Dhaka.

lessons.title: The Simla Delegation and the Birth of the Muslim League
lessons.notes_html:
In 1906 a 35-member delegation of Muslim leaders, led by Sir Aga Khan, met Viceroy Lord Minto at Simla. The Simla Delegation demanded: separate electorates for Muslims for all councils, municipal institutions and district boards; representation for Muslims in legislative assemblies beyond their population proportion, considering their historical, political and defence significance; a share in government jobs in proportion to population; Muslim judges in the High Courts and Chief Courts and members of the Viceroy's and Governors' Councils; and financial aid for a Muslim university at Aligarh. Lord Minto promised to consider the demands with sympathy.

Later the same year, during the Muhammadan Educational Conference session at Dhaka, the All India Muslim League was established on December 30, 1906. Its first formal meeting was held later at Karachi on December 29–30, 1907.

mcqs.q: Under whose leadership did the Muslim delegation meet Lord Minto in 1906?
mcqs.why: The 35-member Simla Delegation was led by Sir Aga Khan when it presented Muslim demands to Viceroy Lord Minto in 1906.

mcqs.q: How many members were there in the Simla Delegation?
mcqs.why: The Simla Delegation consisted of 35 members led by Sir Aga Khan, and Lord Minto promised to consider its demands with sympathy.

mcqs.q: What was the first demand of the Simla Delegation?
options: Separate electorates for Muslims at all levels
mcqs.why: The delegation's first demand was separate electorates for all councils, municipal institutions and district boards, so Muslim voters would elect Muslim candidates.

mcqs.q: The Simla Delegation asked for Muslim representation in legislatures:
options: Beyond population proportion, due to their historical and political significance
mcqs.why: Considering their historical, political and defence significance, the delegation demanded more representation for Muslims than their population proportion alone would give.

mcqs.q: Which demand of the Simla Delegation concerned Aligarh?
options: Financial aid for a Muslim university
mcqs.why: The delegation demanded financial aid for the establishment of a Muslim University at Aligarh, along with jobs, judgeships and council membership for Muslims.

mcqs.q: When and where was the All India Muslim League established?
mcqs.why: The All India Muslim League was formally established at Dhaka on December 30, 1906, during the Muhammadan Educational Conference session.

mcqs.q: Where was the first formal meeting of the Muslim League held after its establishment?
mcqs.why: Although the League was established at Dhaka in 1906, the book notes its first formal meeting was held later at Karachi on December 29–30, 1907.

mcqs.q: How did Lord Minto respond to the Simla Delegation?
options: He promised to consider the demands with sympathy
He referred them to London without comment
mcqs.why: Lord Minto received the delegation favourably and promised to consider the Muslim demands with sympathy, encouraging Muslims to organise politically.

mcqs.q: The Simla Delegation also demanded a Muslim share in:
options: Government jobs in proportion to population
mcqs.why: The delegation demanded that Muslims be given a share in government jobs in proportion to their population, plus Muslim judges and council members.

mcqs.q: The Simla Delegation met the Viceroy at:
mcqs.why: The delegation of Muslim leaders met Lord Minto at Simla in 1906, which is why it is remembered as the Simla Delegation.

lessons.title: Objectives of the Congress and the Muslim League
lessons.notes_html:
The objectives of the Congress were: Indians should be given representation in the government; a legislative council should be formed including representatives of the Indian people; the maximum number of Indians should be included in high government positions, with competitive examinations for the Civil Services held in India; and representative institutions should be established to pave the way for self-governance.

The objectives and goals of the Muslim League were: (1) to create a sense of loyalty towards the British government among the Muslims of India and to remove any doubts or suspicions arising from government actions; (2) to protect the political rights and interests of the Indian Muslims and present their demands to the government; and (3) to foster cooperation and harmony between Muslims and other communities of India, without compromising the first two objectives.

mcqs.q: What was the first objective of the Muslim League regarding the British government?
options: To create loyalty among Muslims towards the British government
mcqs.why: The League's first objective was to create a sense of loyalty towards the British government among Indian Muslims and remove misunderstandings about government actions.

mcqs.q: The Muslim League was formed to protect:
options: The political rights and interests of Indian Muslims
mcqs.why: Protecting the political rights and interests of the Indian Muslims and presenting their demands to the government was a central objective of the Muslim League.

mcqs.q: The third objective of the Muslim League concerned other communities. It was to:
options: Compete with them in elections only
Foster cooperation and harmony with them
mcqs.why: The League also aimed to foster cooperation and harmony between Muslims and other communities of India, without compromising its first two objectives.

mcqs.q: Which of these was an objective of the Congress?
mcqs.why: The Congress objectives included representation of Indians in the government, a legislative council with Indian representatives and self-governance through representative institutions.

mcqs.q: How did the early objectives of the Congress and the Muslim League differ?
options: Congress wanted self-governance; the League focused on loyalty and safeguarding Muslim rights
mcqs.why: The Congress pressed for representation and self-governance, while the young Muslim League emphasised loyalty to the government and protection of Muslim political rights.

mcqs.q: The Muslim League would present Muslim demands to:
mcqs.why: A stated goal of the Muslim League was to protect Muslim rights and present Muslim demands and needs to the government.

mcqs.q: Which demand appears in the Congress objectives but reflects a service reform?
options: Civil Services examinations held in India
mcqs.why: The Congress demanded that the maximum number of Indians enter high government positions and that competitive Civil Services examinations be held in India.

mcqs.q: The League's harmony objective was qualified by the condition that it should not compromise:
options: The first two objectives — loyalty and Muslim rights
mcqs.why: Cooperation with other communities was to be fostered 'without compromising the above objectives' — loyalty to the government and protection of Muslim rights.

mcqs.q: The Congress aimed to pave the way for self-governance through:
mcqs.why: The Congress wanted representative institutions established in India to pave the way for self-governance.

mcqs.q: Removing doubts and suspicions arising from government actions was part of which objective?
mcqs.why: The League's first objective included eliminating any doubts or suspicions among Muslims arising from actions of the British government.

lessons.title: The Minto-Morley Reforms and the Annulment of the Partition
lessons.notes_html:
The Minto-Morley Reforms were passed on November 15, 1909. Their key points were: Indians would be included in the Executive Council of the Governor-General and the Provincial Governors' Executive Councils; the number of members in the Central Legislative Council was increased to 60; the membership of the Provincial Legislative Councils was also increased; the Legislative Councils were granted broader powers, and members were allowed to discuss the budget in detail, ask questions and present resolutions on public issues; and the principle of separate electorates for Muslims was recognised, under which Muslim voters would elect Muslim candidates.

The book notes that through these reforms it was acknowledged for the first time that Hindus and Muslims were two entirely distinct nations. In 1911, however, the partition of Bengal was annulled, which disappointed the Muslims deeply.

lessons.title: Causes of the First World War
lessons.notes_html:
The book gives these main causes of the First World War (1914–18):

(1) Secret treaties and the arms race: in 1879 Germany signed a treaty with Austria-Hungary and Italy later joined, forming the Triple Alliance, while Britain, France and Russia formed the Entente Cordiale. The race to build warships, modern weapons and military technology created tension and fear.

(2) Aggressive nationalism: many European nations believed their culture, race or country was superior; Germany and Austria hated the Slavs, while Serbian nationalism wanted to free the Serbs from Austria-Hungary.

(3) The immediate cause: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austrian throne, on June 28, 1914. He and his wife were assassinated in Bosnia by a member of a Serbian terrorist organisation. Austria decided to crush Serbia, Germany announced support for Austria, Russia decided to support Serbia, and the armies began to mobilise, so a small incident turned into a world war.

mcqs.q: In which year did the First World War begin?
mcqs.why: The First World War began in 1914, following the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and the mobilisation of the rival alliance systems.

options: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The sinking of a British ship
mcqs.why: The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austrian throne, in Bosnia on June 28, 1914.

mcqs.q: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated on:
mcqs.why: Franz Ferdinand and his wife were assassinated on June 28, 1914, in Bosnia by a member of a Serbian terrorist organisation.

mcqs.why: Germany signed a treaty with Austria-Hungary in 1879 and Italy joined later, forming the Triple Alliance against the rival Entente of Britain, France and Russia.

mcqs.q: Britain, France and Russia grouped together in the:
mcqs.why: Britain, France and Russia formed the Entente Cordiale, the alliance bloc that opposed the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.

mcqs.q: How did aggressive nationalism contribute to the war?
options: Nations believed their culture or race was superior and hated rivals
mcqs.why: Aggressive nationalism made nations believe their culture, race or country was superior; Germany and Austria hated the Slavs, and Serbian nationalism sought freedom from Austria-Hungary.

mcqs.why: Austria decided to crush Serbia after the assassination; Germany supported Austria, Russia supported Serbia, and mobilisation turned the crisis into a world war.

mcqs.why: Russia decided to support Serbia, while Germany announced support for Austria — the alliance system pulled all the great powers into the war.

mcqs.why: The race to build warships, modern weapons and military technology — the arms race — created tension and fear that helped cause the war.

mcqs.why: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was heir to the Austrian throne; his assassination in Bosnia set off the chain of events that began the First World War.

lessons.title: The Ottoman Empire Joins the War
lessons.notes_html:
The Ottoman Empire joined the war on Germany's side. Its reasons were: to restore the dignity of the Empire and gain independence from the Western powers, to recapture Egypt and Cyprus, and to free Turkestan from Russian control and re-establish the Caliphate as a central power in the Islamic world.

On August 2, 1914, the Ottomans signed a secret alliance treaty with Germany, and on October 29, 1914, the Ottoman navy attacked Russian ships in the Black Sea, officially entering the war. Before entering, the Ottoman Caliph declared Jihad and appealed to Muslims worldwide to support the Ottomans — a matter of deep concern for the Muslims of India, who revered the Caliphate.

mcqs.q: On which side did the Ottoman Empire fight in the First World War?
mcqs.why: The Ottoman Empire supported Germany in the First World War, signing a secret alliance with it on August 2, 1914.

mcqs.q: Why did the Ottoman Empire join the war?
options: To restore the Empire's dignity and recapture Egypt and Cyprus
To gain colonies in Africa only
mcqs.why: The Ottomans joined Germany to restore the Empire's dignity, win independence from Western powers, recapture Egypt and Cyprus and free Turkestan from Russia.

mcqs.q: When did the Ottomans sign their secret alliance treaty with Germany?
mcqs.why: The Ottoman Empire signed a secret alliance treaty with Germany on August 2, 1914, weeks before formally entering the war.

mcqs.q: How did the Ottoman Empire officially enter the war?
options: Its navy attacked Russian ships in the Black Sea
mcqs.why: On October 29, 1914, the Ottoman navy attacked Russian ships in the Black Sea, which officially brought the Empire into the war.

mcqs.q: The Ottoman attack on Russian ships took place on:
mcqs.why: The Ottoman navy attacked Russian ships in the Black Sea on October 29, 1914, formally opening the Empire's participation in the war.

mcqs.q: Before entering the war, the Ottoman Caliph declared:
options: Jihad, appealing to Muslims worldwide for support
mcqs.why: The Ottoman Caliph declared Jihad and appealed to Muslims worldwide to support the Ottomans, which deeply concerned the Muslims of India.

mcqs.q: Which territories did the Ottomans hope to recapture from Western control?
mcqs.why: The Ottomans hoped to recapture Egypt and Cyprus and to free Turkestan from Russian control, restoring the Caliphate as a central Islamic power.

mcqs.why: One Ottoman aim was to free Turkestan from Russian control and re-establish the Caliphate as a central power in the Islamic world.

options: They revered the Ottoman Caliphate and its holy places
They served in the German army
mcqs.why: Indian Muslims held the Ottoman Caliphate in great esteem and feared for the holy places, so the Empire's entry into the war against Britain placed them in a painful dilemma.

mcqs.q: The Ottoman-German alliance of 1914 was:
mcqs.why: The alliance signed on August 2, 1914 was a secret treaty; the Empire only entered open war with the Black Sea attack of October 29, 1914.

lessons.title: America Enters and Russia Withdraws
lessons.notes_html:
Two events of 1917 transformed the war. In Russia, the Bolshevik Revolution overthrew the Tsar; the new communist government signed a treaty with Germany and withdrew from the war. After the revolution a civil war broke out in Russia; America, Japan, France and Britain sent troops against the Bolshevik government but failed. On July 16, 1918, the Russian Tsar and his family were executed. The Bolshevik Party was renamed the Communist Party, and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) was founded, with Russia and its former territories as part of the Union.

In the same year the United States joined the war — the U.S. Congress approved the declaration of war against Germany on April 6, 1917. America's involvement tilted the balance in favour of Britain and its allies, because the United States provided extensive supplies of weapons and other materials. When fresh American troops attacked Germany, Germany was unable to fight and ultimately surrendered in November 1918; Emperor Wilhelm II abdicated on November 9, 1918, and Germany signed an armistice with the Allies.

mcqs.q: In which year did the United States join the First World War?
mcqs.why: The United States joined the war in 1917; the U.S. Congress approved the declaration of war against Germany on April 6, 1917.

mcqs.q: When did the U.S. Congress approve the declaration of war against Germany?
mcqs.why: The U.S. Congress approved the declaration of war against Germany on April 6, 1917, bringing fresh troops and supplies to the Allied side.

mcqs.q: Russia withdrew from the war after which event?
mcqs.why: After the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917, the new communist government signed a treaty with Germany and withdrew Russia from the war.

mcqs.q: In which year did Russia leave the First World War?
mcqs.why: The unit text places Russia's revolution and its decision to leave the war in 1917, after which it signed a treaty with Germany.

mcqs.q: What happened to the Russian Tsar and his family?
mcqs.why: After the revolution and civil war, the Russian Tsar and his family were executed on July 16, 1918, ending the Tsarist monarchy.

mcqs.q: The Bolshevik Party was renamed as the:
mcqs.why: The Bolshevik Party was renamed the Communist Party, and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) was founded from Russia and its former territories.

mcqs.q: What was the union formed from Russia and its former territories called?
mcqs.why: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) was founded with Russia and its former territories as part of the Union, as recorded in the book.

mcqs.q: How did America's entry change the war?
options: It tilted the balance in favour of Britain and its allies
mcqs.why: America's involvement tilted the balance in favour of Britain and its allies through extensive supplies of weapons and fresh troops.

mcqs.q: When did Germany surrender and sign the armistice?
mcqs.why: Germany surrendered in November 1918; Emperor Wilhelm II abdicated on November 9, 1918, and Germany signed an armistice with the Allies.

mcqs.q: Which countries sent troops against the new Bolshevik government during Russia's civil war?
mcqs.why: America, Japan, France and Britain sent troops against the Bolshevik government during the Russian civil war, but they failed to defeat it.

lessons.title: The End of the War and the Peace Settlement
lessons.notes_html:
The war killed nearly 10 million people and dissolved the Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and German empires and the Russian Tsarist monarchy. The Paris Peace Conference opened on January 18, 1919.

The United States played the leading peace role: President Woodrow Wilson presented his famous 14 Points for lasting peace, which included open diplomacy, the right of nations to self-determination, the abolition of arms races, freedom of navigation on the seas, free trade and the creation of an international organisation — the League of Nations — to guarantee world freedom and peace. The Treaty of Versailles (June 28, 1919) also established the League of Nations to promote peace and collective security. At Paris, British Prime Minister Lloyd George supported more lenient terms for Germany, while French Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau wanted harsh terms so Germany could never threaten France again.

mcqs.q: Approximately how many people were killed in the First World War?
mcqs.why: The war killed nearly 10 million people and dissolved the Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and German empires and the Russian Tsarist monarchy.

mcqs.q: When did the Paris Peace Conference open?
mcqs.why: The Paris Peace Conference was held from January 18, 1919, to settle the terms of peace after the First World War.

mcqs.q: Who presented the famous 14 Points for lasting peace?
mcqs.why: U.S. President Woodrow Wilson presented his 14 Points, including open diplomacy, self-determination and a League of Nations.

mcqs.q: Which organisation did Wilson's 14 Points propose to create?
mcqs.why: The 14 Points proposed an international organisation, the League of Nations, to guarantee world freedom and peace; the Treaty of Versailles established it.

mcqs.q: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in:
mcqs.why: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on June 28, 1919, and it also established the League of Nations for peace and collective security.

mcqs.q: Which peace delegate wanted harsh terms for Germany so it could never threaten his country again?
mcqs.why: French Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau wanted harsh terms for Germany, while Britain's Lloyd George supported more lenient terms.

mcqs.q: Which leader supported more lenient terms for Germany at Paris?
mcqs.why: British Prime Minister Lloyd George supported more lenient terms for Germany at the Paris Peace Conference, against Clemenceau's demand for harsh terms.

options: Freedom of navigation on the seas
mcqs.why: The 14 Points included open diplomacy, self-determination, abolition of arms races, freedom of navigation on the seas and free trade.

mcqs.q: Which empires dissolved as a result of the First World War?
options: The Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and German empires
mcqs.why: The war dissolved the Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and German empires and ended the Russian Tsarist monarchy.

mcqs.q: The League of Nations was created to promote:
mcqs.why: The League of Nations was established by the Treaty of Versailles to promote peace and collective security among nations.

lessons.title: The Treaty of Sevres and the Treaty of Lausanne
lessons.notes_html:
The Treaty of Sevres was signed on August 10, 1920, at Sevres, France, after Germany's defeat and the Arab revolt forced the Ottomans to sign. Its key points were: (1) the state of Hejaz would operate under the control of Britain; (2) an independent Christian state would be established in Armenia; (3) France would take control of Syria; (4) the territories of Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon and Palestine would be handed over to the Allies; (5) Cyprus, Smyrna and the region of Asia Minor would come under the control of Greece; and (6) Turkey would pay a specified amount as war reparations.

Muslims worldwide protested against this unfair agreement. Mustafa Kemal Pasha refused to accept it, defeated the Greeks, and a new Treaty of Lausanne was signed in 1923, under which Turkey regained Thrace and Smyrna.

mcqs.q: When was the Treaty of Sevres signed?
mcqs.why: The Treaty of Sevres was signed on August 10, 1920, at Sevres in France, imposing harsh terms on the defeated Ottoman Empire.

mcqs.q: Under Sevres, which country would take control of Syria?
mcqs.why: The Treaty of Sevres gave France control of Syria, while Hejaz was to operate under British control and other Ottoman lands went to the Allies or Greece.

mcqs.q: Which territories did Sevres hand over to the Allies?
mcqs.why: Under Sevres, the territories of Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon and Palestine were handed over to the Allies, dismembering the Ottoman Empire.

mcqs.q: Under the Treaty of Sevres, Cyprus and Smyrna were to come under the control of:
mcqs.why: Sevres placed Cyprus, Smyrna and the region of Asia Minor under the control of Greece, which provoked Turkish resistance under Mustafa Kemal.

mcqs.q: Sevres proposed an independent Christian state in:
mcqs.why: Among the key points of Sevres was the establishment of an independent Christian state in Armenia, carved out of Ottoman territory.

mcqs.q: Who refused to accept the Treaty of Sevres and defeated the Greeks?
mcqs.why: Mustafa Kemal Pasha refused to accept the unfair Treaty of Sevres, defeated the Greeks and forced the Allies to negotiate a new treaty.

mcqs.q: Which treaty replaced Sevres in 1923?
mcqs.why: The Treaty of Lausanne was signed in 1923 after Mustafa Kemal's victories, replacing the Treaty of Sevres on far better terms for Turkey.

mcqs.q: Under the Treaty of Lausanne, Turkey regained:
mcqs.why: Under the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) Turkey regained Thrace and Smyrna, undoing the harshest territorial losses imposed by Sevres.

mcqs.q: How did Muslims worldwide react to the Treaty of Sevres?
options: They protested against the unfair agreement
mcqs.why: Muslims worldwide protested against the unfair Treaty of Sevres, which dismembered the Ottoman Caliphate's lands among the victorious powers.

mcqs.q: Under Sevres, Turkey was also required to:
options: Pay a specified amount as war reparations
mcqs.why: The Treaty of Sevres required Turkey to pay a specified amount as war reparations, in addition to losing its Arab and other territories.

lessons.title: India's Role in the First World War
lessons.notes_html:
Almost all political parties and leaders in India announced their support for the British government during the First World War, and a fund was established for the war effort. Gandhi helped in recruiting Indian soldiers and established an ambulance corps, while the British also used forced recruitment in Punjab.

Around 1.5 million Indian soldiers participated in the war, serving in France, Belgium, Egypt, Sudan, Africa, Iran, Iraq, Palestine and China; by the end of the war 74,000 Indian soldiers had been killed and nearly 65,000 wounded. About 13 million pounds in war expenses were paid from the Indian treasury. Indian Muslims, however, remained concerned about the future of the Ottoman Caliphate and the Holy Places, since Britain was fighting against the Ottoman Empire.

mcqs.q: Approximately how many Indian soldiers participated in the First World War?
mcqs.why: Around 1.5 million Indian soldiers participated in the war, serving in France, Belgium, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Palestine, China and elsewhere.

mcqs.q: How many Indian soldiers were killed in the First World War?
mcqs.why: By the end of the war 74,000 Indian soldiers had been killed and nearly 65,000 wounded, out of about 1.5 million who served.

mcqs.q: What role did Gandhi play during the war?
options: He helped recruit Indian soldiers and set up an ambulance corps
mcqs.why: Gandhi helped in recruiting Indian soldiers and established an ambulance corps, while almost all Indian parties announced support for the British war effort.

mcqs.q: How much of the war expenses was paid from the Indian treasury?
mcqs.why: About 13 million pounds in war expenses were paid from the Indian treasury, besides the huge human contribution of Indian soldiers.

mcqs.q: In which province did the British also use forced recruitment?
mcqs.why: Besides voluntary support, the British used forced recruitment in Punjab to raise soldiers for the war effort.

mcqs.q: Indian Muslims remained concerned during the war about:
options: The future of the Ottoman Caliphate and the Holy Places
mcqs.why: Indian Muslims remained concerned about the future of the Ottoman Caliphate and the Holy Places, because Britain was at war with the Ottoman Empire.

mcqs.q: In which of these regions did Indian soldiers NOT serve, according to the book's list?
mcqs.why: Indian soldiers served in France, Belgium, Egypt, Sudan, Africa, Iran, Iraq, Palestine and China; Japan is not in the book's list of their theatres of service.

mcqs.q: Nearly how many Indian soldiers were wounded in the war?
mcqs.why: Nearly 65,000 Indian soldiers were wounded in the First World War, in addition to the 74,000 who were killed.

mcqs.q: Almost all Indian political parties and leaders announced what at the start of the war?
mcqs.why: Almost all political parties and leaders in India announced their support for the British government, and a fund was established for the war effort.

mcqs.q: The concern of Indian Muslims during the war later grew into which movement?
mcqs.why: Muslim concern for the Ottoman Caliphate and the holy places grew after the war into the Khilafat Movement, a major cause of Hindu-Muslim unity in 1919–22.

lessons.title: The Lucknow Pact 1916
lessons.notes_html:
The Lucknow Pact was approved in December 1916 at the joint Lucknow sessions of the Muslim League and the Congress, through the efforts of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah, whom Sarojini Naidu called the 'best ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity'.

Its key points were: the Congress recognised the Muslims' right to separate electorates; Muslim representation in Muslim-majority provinces was fixed at 50% in Punjab and 40% in Bengal, while in Hindu-majority provinces Muslims were given double representation against their population ('weightage'); Muslims would have one-third of the seats in the Central Legislative Council; half of the members of the Central and Provincial Executive Councils would be Indian; and no law would be considered if three-fourths of the members of a community opposed it.

The pact established Hindu-Muslim unity, which lasted until 1920, and both parties jointly demanded reforms from the government — though Muslims paid a price by forgoing their majority status in Punjab and Bengal.

mcqs.q: When was the Lucknow Pact signed between the Muslim League and the Congress?
mcqs.why: The Lucknow Pact was approved in December 1916 at the joint Lucknow sessions of the Muslim League and the Congress.

mcqs.q: Through whose efforts was the Lucknow Pact achieved?
mcqs.why: The Lucknow Pact was achieved through the efforts of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the architect of the 1916 agreement.

mcqs.q: Who called Jinnah the 'best ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity'?
mcqs.why: Sarojini Naidu called Muhammad Ali Jinnah the best ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity for his role in bringing about the Lucknow Pact.

mcqs.q: Under the Lucknow Pact, the Congress recognised the Muslims' right to:
mcqs.why: For the first time the Congress recognised the Muslims' right to separate electorates, accepting them as a distinct political community.

mcqs.q: Muslim representation in Punjab and Bengal was fixed under the pact at:
mcqs.why: The pact fixed Muslim representation at 50% in Punjab and 40% in Bengal — below their population majority, a price Muslims paid for the unity agreement.

mcqs.q: What share of seats in the Central Legislative Council would Muslims have under the pact?
mcqs.why: The Lucknow Pact provided that Muslims would have one-third of the seats in the Central Legislative Council.

mcqs.q: The 'weightage' principle in the pact meant that in Hindu-majority provinces Muslims would get:
mcqs.why: Under weightage, Muslims in Hindu-majority provinces were given double representation against their population, balancing their reduced shares in Punjab and Bengal.

mcqs.q: Under the pact, a law would not be considered if what proportion of a community's members opposed it?
mcqs.why: The pact provided that no law would be considered if three-fourths of the members of a community opposed it — a communal veto safeguard.

mcqs.q: The Lucknow Pact's Hindu-Muslim unity lasted until about:
mcqs.why: The unity established by the Lucknow Pact lasted until 1920, and during it both parties jointly demanded reforms from the government.

mcqs.q: What price did Muslims pay in the Lucknow Pact?
options: They accepted less than their majority share in Punjab and Bengal
mcqs.why: Muslims paid a price in the pact by forgoing their majority status in Punjab and Bengal, accepting 50% and 40% representation there.

lessons.title: The Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
lessons.notes_html:
The Rowlatt Act was passed by the Central Legislative Council in 1919 on the report of a committee chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt. Its key provisions were: any Indian could be arrested without being told the reasons; the prosecution would not be required to prove the charges; the burden of proof would be on the defendant, who could be punished without evidence; the accused could be sentenced without any witness testimony; hearings would be conducted in closed rooms; and those convicted would have no right to appeal. Muhammad Ali Jinnah, a member of the Central Legislative Council, declared the Act a violation of human rights and the principles of justice and resigned from the Council in protest; Mazhar-ul-Haq also resigned.

Jallianwala Bagh

On April 9, 1919, two Satyagraha leaders, Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satya Pal, were arrested in Amritsar and protests broke out. The Governor of Punjab, Michael O'Dwyer, handed the city to Brigadier General Reginald Dyer. A gathering was announced at Jallianwala Bagh on April 13, 1919 — also the Baisakhi festival — in an open ground surrounded by houses with only one narrow entrance. Dyer arrived with his troops and ordered them to open fire on the crowd without warning; the soldiers fired for ten minutes, shooting 1,650 rounds. According to official statistics, 379 people were killed and 1,200 injured. A curfew followed and martial law was declared; the Hunter Commission later absolved the Governor and the Viceroy, and Dyer was only compulsorily retired. The brutality caused widespread shock and anger and fuelled the independence movement in India.

mcqs.why: The Rowlatt Act was passed in 1919 by the Central Legislative Council on the report of the committee chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt.

mcqs.q: The Rowlatt Act committee was chaired by:
mcqs.why: The Act was based on the report (published April 25, 1918) of a committee chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt, after whom it is named.

mcqs.why: The Rowlatt Act allowed punishment without evidence, put the burden of proof on the defendant, held hearings in closed rooms and gave no right of appeal.

mcqs.q: How did Muhammad Ali Jinnah react to the Rowlatt Act?

mcqs.why: Jinnah, a member of the Central Legislative Council, declared the Act a violation of human rights and justice and resigned from the Council as soon as it was passed.

mcqs.why: Another prominent Muslim leader, Mazhar-ul-Haq, also resigned from the Legislative Council in protest against the Rowlatt Act.

mcqs.q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on:
mcqs.why: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on April 13, 1919, the day of the Baisakhi festival, in Amritsar.

mcqs.q: Who ordered the troops to open fire at Jallianwala Bagh?
mcqs.why: Brigadier General Reginald Dyer arrived with his troops and ordered them to open fire on the crowd without warning, firing 1,650 rounds in ten minutes.

mcqs.q: According to official statistics, how many people were killed at Jallianwala Bagh?
mcqs.why: According to official statistics 379 people were killed and 1,200 injured at Jallianwala Bagh; 1,650 was the number of rounds fired.

mcqs.q: How many rounds did Dyer's soldiers fire at Jallianwala Bagh?
mcqs.why: The soldiers fired for ten minutes, shooting 1,650 rounds into the trapped crowd in the enclosed Bagh.

mcqs.why: The Hunter Commission absolved the Governor and the Viceroy, and Dyer was only compulsorily retired — a mild outcome that deepened Indian anger.

lessons.title: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms 1919
lessons.notes_html: The Government of India Act 1919, prepared under Governor-General Lord Chelmsford and Secretary of State Montagu, provided: (1) the Secretary of State for India would now be paid from the British Treasury; (2) a bicameral legislature (Imperial Legislative Council) was created at the centre, consisting of the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly, whose members would be elected through separate electorates, with 30 seats reserved for Muslims and 2 for Sikhs, and a term of 3 years; (3) powers were divided between the centre (defence, foreign affairs, communications, currency, finance, railways, telegraph, religious affairs, civil services) and the provinces (law and order, justice, prisons, irrigation, agriculture, education, local self-governance); (4) a unicameral legislature was maintained in the provinces with increased membership, but no law could be enforced without the Governor's approval; (5) a dual system — Dyarchy — was introduced in the provinces, dividing departments into reserved (controlled by the Governor) and transferred (run by ministers from the elected assembly); and (6) ten years after implementation, a Royal Commission would review the reforms.

mcqs.q: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms are contained in which act?
mcqs.why: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms formed the Government of India Act 1919, prepared under Lord Chelmsford and Secretary of State Montagu.

mcqs.q: What kind of legislature was created at the centre by the 1919 Act?

mcqs.why: The 1919 Act created a bicameral Imperial Legislative Council at the centre, consisting of the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly.

mcqs.q: How many seats were reserved for Muslims in the central legislature under the 1919 Act?
mcqs.why: Members of the central legislature were elected through separate electorates, with 30 seats reserved for Muslims and 2 for Sikhs, for a term of 3 years.

mcqs.q: What was the term of the central legislature under the 1919 Act?
mcqs.why: The Council of State and the Legislative Assembly created by the 1919 Act had a term of 3 years.

mcqs.q: The dual system introduced in the provinces by the 1919 Act was called:
mcqs.why: Dyarchy divided provincial departments into reserved subjects controlled by the Governor and transferred subjects run by ministers from the elected assembly.

mcqs.why: Transferred departments were run by ministers drawn from the elected provincial assembly, while reserved departments stayed under the Governor's control.

options: Defence, foreign affairs, currency and railways
mcqs.why: The centre retained defence, foreign affairs, communications, currency, finance, railways, telegraph, religious affairs and the civil services.

mcqs.q: Which subjects were given to the provinces under the 1919 Act?
options: Law and order, justice, irrigation, agriculture and education
mcqs.why: Provincial subjects included law and order, justice, prisons, irrigation, agriculture, education and local self-governance.

mcqs.q: After how many years was a Royal Commission to review the 1919 reforms?
mcqs.why: The 1919 Act provided that ten years after implementation a Royal Commission would review the reforms — this led to the Simon Commission.

mcqs.why: Provincial legislatures were unicameral with increased membership, but no law could be enforced without the Governor's approval.

lessons.title: The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movements
lessons.notes_html:
The Khilafat Movement was started because Indian Muslims held the Ottoman Caliphate in great esteem and feared that if Turkey lost the war, Britain and France might capture the holy places (Makkah, Madinah, Jerusalem, Syria, Iraq) and the collapse of the Caliphate would end Islam's centre of authority. Leaders such as Maulana Mohammad Ali Jouhar, Maulana Shaukat Ali, Maulana Zafar Ali Khan, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and Maulana Hasrat Mohani raised awareness; the Khilafat Committee was formed at Lucknow on September 22, 1919, and after Lloyd George rejected the Khilafat delegation's demands, a nationwide strike was held on March 19, 1920, and the Non-Cooperation Movement was announced.

Gandhi's Non-Cooperation plan was: return all titles and medals conferred by the British government, resign from nominated local bodies and boycott government functions; boycott schools, colleges and courts; boycott the elections under the 1919 reforms; and boycott foreign goods. Hindus and Muslims participated enthusiastically together.

The Hijrat Movement and the failure of Khilafat

In 1920 some Muslim scholars issued a fatwa declaring India 'Dar-ul-Harb'; influenced by it, many Muslims sold their properties at low prices and migrated towards Afghanistan. The movement, concentrated in Sindh and Punjab, failed miserably: the migrants suffered severe losses and had to return. The Khilafat Movement finally failed because the Hijrat Movement spread disappointment; after the Chauri Chaura incident of February 5, 1922, Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement, which was the soul of the Khilafat Movement; its prominent leaders were in jail; and finally Mustafa Kemal Pasha abolished the Caliphate itself on March 3, 1924.

lessons.title: The Simon Commission and the Delhi Proposals
lessons.notes_html:
The Government of India Act 1919 had stated that after ten years a commission would review the reforms and recommend further steps. A seven-member commission was therefore formed under the headship of Sir John Simon. Its objective was to examine how the 1919 reforms had worked and to recommend the next constitutional steps for India. But all its members were British and no Indian was included, so all political parties in India boycotted it.

The Commission arrived in Bombay on February 3, 1928, and wherever it went it was greeted with black flags and slogans of 'Simon Go Back'; violent protests occurred in Lucknow, Delhi and Lahore, and on February 16, 1928, a resolution against it was passed in the Central Legislative Assembly. Despite the opposition, it completed its work, left India on April 13, 1929, and its report was published in May 1930.

In the Delhi Proposals of 1927, the Muslims offered to withdraw from the demand for separate electorates on certain conditions — a significant Muslim attempt at a constitutional settlement in this period.

lessons.title: The Nehru Report and the Muslim Reaction
lessons.notes_html:
The Nehru Report (1928), drafted by a committee presided over by Motilal Nehru, proposed: (1) the separate electorate system for Muslims should be abolished as it harms Indian nationality; (2) no specific seat allocation in the Punjab and Bengal assemblies based on population quotas; (3) in Muslim-minority provinces, Muslims should get seats according to their population, with the right to contest general seats, and a similar provision for Hindus in the North-Western Province; (4) one-third representation for Muslims in the Central Legislative Assembly was denied — only 25% of seats were recommended according to population; (5) Sindh's separation was accepted if it could bear the financial burden; (6) full provincial autonomy for the North-Western Province and Balochistan was acknowledged; and (7) a strong central (unitary) government was recommended for India.

The report deeply disappointed Muslim leaders who had worked for Hindu-Muslim unity. Shoaib Qureshi, the only Muslim member of the committee, wrote a dissenting note. Quaid-e-Azam concluded that Muslims and Hindus had parted ways, and on January 1, 1929, the All Parties Muslim Conference at Delhi — convened by Maulana Muhammad Ali Jouhar and presided over by the Aga Khan — unanimously rejected the Nehru Report.

mcqs.why: The Nehru Report was published in 1928, drafted by a committee presided over by Motilal Nehru in response to the constitutional question.

mcqs.why: The Nehru Report was drafted by a committee presided over by Motilal Nehru, father of Jawaharlal Nehru.

mcqs.why: The Nehru Report proposed abolishing the separate electorate system for Muslims, calling it harmful to the development of Indian nationality.

mcqs.why: The report denied the Muslim demand for one-third representation at the centre and recommended only 25% of seats according to population.

mcqs.why: The Nehru Report recommended a strong central government for India — a unitary form — against the Muslim demand for a federation with autonomous provinces.

options: Shoaib Qureshi wrote a dissenting note
mcqs.why: Shoaib Qureshi, the only Muslim member of the committee, wrote a dissenting note against the report's treatment of Muslim demands.

That Muslims and Hindus had parted ways
mcqs.why: Quaid-e-Azam concluded that the Nehru Report showed Muslims and Hindus had parted ways, ending his efforts at a Congress-League settlement on those terms.

mcqs.why: The All Parties Muslim Conference was held at Delhi on January 1, 1929, convened by Maulana Muhammad Ali Jouhar and presided over by the Aga Khan.

mcqs.why: The All Parties Muslim Conference of January 1, 1929, unanimously rejected the Nehru Report, uniting Muslim opinion against it.

mcqs.why: The demand to make Sindh a separate province was accepted in the report, provided Sindh could financially bear the burden of a separate province.

lessons.title: Jinnah's Fourteen Points
lessons.notes_html:
Muhammad Ali Jinnah presented the Fourteen Points in March 1929, at the Delhi session of the All India Muslim League, in response to the Nehru Report, which had attempted to undermine Muslim interests by abolishing separate electorates, denying one-third Muslim representation in the Central Legislative Assembly and recommending a strong central government. The resolution stated that no constitution for India would be acceptable to Muslims unless these points were included.

The Fourteen Points in brief

(1) A federal constitution with residuary powers vested in the provinces; (2) equal autonomy for all provinces; (3) adequate and effective minority representation without reducing any majority to a minority; (4) Muslim representation in the Central Legislative Assembly not less than one-third; (5) no reduction of the Muslim majority in Punjab, Bengal and the NWFP in any reorganisation; (6) separate electorates retained, with the option to switch to joint electorates; (7) full religious freedom for all communities; (8) no law passed if three-fourths of a community's members oppose it; (9) Sindh separated from Bombay as a distinct province; (10) full reforms in the NWFP and Balochistan; (11) protection of Muslim culture, education, language, religion and personal laws; (12) at least one-third Muslim ministers in central and provincial governments; (13) no constitutional amendment by the centre without the provinces' and minorities' approval; (14) a fair share for Muslims in government employment.

mcqs.why: Jinnah presented the Fourteen Points in March 1929 at the Delhi session of the All India Muslim League, in response to the Nehru Report.

mcqs.q: The Fourteen Points were presented in response to:
mcqs.why: The Fourteen Points answered the Nehru Report, which had abolished separate electorates, denied one-third central representation and proposed a strong centre.

Federal, with residuary powers vested in the provinces
mcqs.why: The first point demanded a federal constitution for India with the remaining (residuary) powers vested in the provinces, not the centre.

mcqs.why: Point 4 demanded that Muslim representation in the Central Legislative Assembly should not be less than one-third.

mcqs.why: Point 6 retained the separate electorate system, while allowing minorities the option to switch to a joint electorate at any time.

mcqs.why: Point 9 demanded that Sindh should be separated from Bombay and made a distinct province — a long-standing Muslim demand.

mcqs.why: Point 10 demanded that full reforms should be introduced in the North-West Frontier Province and Balochistan, like other provinces.

mcqs.q: What proportion of ministers in central and provincial governments were to be Muslim?
mcqs.why: Point 12 demanded that at least one-third of the ministers in the central and provincial governments should be Muslim.

mcqs.q: Under the Fourteen Points, a law could not be passed if opposed by:
mcqs.why: Point 8 provided that no law should be passed in any elected body unless three-fourths of the members of a community approve it — the old Lucknow Pact safeguard.

mcqs.q: The Fourteen Points stated that no constitution would be acceptable to Muslims unless:
options: These points protecting Muslim rights were included
mcqs.why: The resolution declared that no constitution for India would be acceptable to Muslims unless the Fourteen Points, protecting Muslim rights and interests, were included.

lessons.title: Allama Iqbal and the Allahabad Address
lessons.notes_html:
The All India Muslim League held its general session at Allahabad on December 29, 1930, presided over by Allama Iqbal. In his presidential address — a historic milestone in the demand for a separate Muslim state — Iqbal emphasised the separate national identity of the Muslims on religious and cultural grounds and argued that Western democracy could not work in a subcontinent of diverse languages, religions and cultures.

He proposed that the Ambala Division be detached and the rest of Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), Balochistan and Sindh be amalgamated to form a single separate Muslim state, saying that a consolidated North-West Indian Muslim state appeared to him to be the final destiny of the Muslims of North-West India.

Allama Iqbal is called 'Shair-e-Mashriq' (Poet of the East) because through his poetry he awakened the Muslims of the East from their decline and gave them the message of selfhood, unity and a separate national identity. The book presents him as the thinker whose ideas, expressed in his poetry and his 1930 Allahabad Address, laid the intellectual foundation of a separate Muslim state.

mcqs.why: The 1930 Allahabad Address laid the intellectual foundation of the demand for a separate Muslim state, presented by Iqbal as its thinker and poet.

lessons.title: The Salt March and Civil Disobedience
lessons.notes_html:
Under a British law of 1882, people were forbidden from making salt from seawater, violation could bring a six-month prison sentence, and the public was forced to buy salt from the government and pay tax on it, which caused public resentment. Gandhi capitalised on this discontent and announced a civil disobedience movement against the salt law.

On March 12, 1930, Gandhi, along with his followers, began a 387-kilometre march from Ahmedabad to Dandi, a coastal town in Surat, covering the distance in 24 days. On April 6, 1930, he reached the sea and picked up natural salt from the shore, violating the 1882 law. The police severely baton-charged Gandhi and his followers, but they did not resist. People across India started producing salt along the coast, the movement received global attention, and women played a significant role in it. During the Second Round Table Conference period, the government negotiated with Gandhi, leading to his release and the end of the movement.

mcqs.why: The salt law dated from 1882; Gandhi chose it as the target of civil disobedience because the salt tax hurt every Indian, rich or poor.

lessons.title: The Round Table Conferences
lessons.notes_html:
Three Round Table Conferences were convened in London in 1930, 1931 and 1932 to decide India's constitutional future. The first conference remained in session from November 12, 1930, to January 19, 1931. Mahatma Gandhi was in jail and the Congress boycotted it because it had started the Civil Disobedience Movement. The Muslim League participated; its representatives included Sir Aga Khan, Sir Muhammad Shafi, Maulvi Fazlul Haq, Maulana Mohammad Ali Jouhar, Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum and Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Sardar Tej Bahadur Sapru, Dr. Ambedkar, Parsi representatives and rulers of the princely states were also present.

All parties agreed to establish an All India Federation, but no progress was made on minority issues. Agreement was reached that the future form of government in India would be federal, the provinces would enjoy complete autonomy, Sindh would be separated from Bombay, and the North-Western Frontier Province would be made a full-fledged province; the British Prime Minister announced the acceptance of these proposals.

mcqs.why: Three Round Table Conferences were convened in London in 1930, 1931 and 1932 to settle India's constitutional future.

mcqs.why: Agreement was reached that Sindh would be separated from Bombay and the North-Western Frontier Province made a full-fledged province.

mcqs.why: No progress was made on minority issues at the first conference — the deadlock over minority safeguards later led to the Communal Award.

lessons.title: The Communal Award and the Poona Pact
lessons.notes_html:
When Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald realised that no compromise could be reached among Indian leaders on protecting minority rights, he announced the Communal Award in August 1932. Its key points were: all minority communities (Muslims, Anglo-Indians, Sikhs, Christians and Dalits) would have the right to separate electorates; one-third of the seats in the Central Legislative Assembly would be reserved for Muslims; in provinces where Muslims were in a minority, they were given more seats than their population ratio; but in Punjab and Bengal, where Muslims were in the majority, they were not given majority representation — Punjab Muslims were 57.5% of the population but received only 49% representation, and in Bengal 46% against a 55% majority. Christians and Anglo-Indians, only about 1% of the population, were given 10% representation, while the League's demand of 33.5% at the centre was not met.

The Poona Pact

The Award had given separate electorates to the Dalits (untouchables), against which Gandhi went on a fast unto death. At last, on December 25, 1932 (as printed in the book), a pact was signed in Poona between the untouchables' leader Dr. B. R. Ambedkar and Gandhi — the Poona Pact. Under it, the Dalits gave up their right to separate electorates; the pact ended Gandhi's fast and gave the depressed classes reserved seats in the provincial legislatures under a joint electorate system.

mcqs.why: British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award in August 1932, when Indian leaders failed to agree on minority rights.

mcqs.why: Gandhi fasted unto death against the Communal Award's grant of separate electorates to the Dalits, fearing it would divide Hindu society.

mcqs.why: The Poona Pact was signed between Gandhi and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, the leader of the untouchables, at Poona.
