lessons.title: The Government of India Act 1935
lessons.notes_html:
The Government of India Act 1935 embodied most of the Round Table Conferences' proposals. Its important points were: (1) it established an All India Federation, including all provinces and states; (2) a federal legislature of two houses — the Council of State and the Federal Assembly; (3) powers were divided between the federal and provincial governments — the federation retained defence, foreign affairs, communications, imports and exports, and currency, while the provinces were granted autonomy over internal affairs, with provincial departments under ministers elected by the provincial assemblies; (4) the head of the federal administration was the Governor-General; (5) Sindh was separated from Bombay and made a separate province (effective 1936); (6) a Federal Court was established at the centre; (7) Muslims were granted one-third representation in the central legislature; (8) the principle of separate electorates was maintained; (9) reforms were introduced in the North-West Frontier Province; and (10) Burma was separated from India.

The federal part of the Act was never implemented, but the provincial part came into force on April 1, 1937, and elections were held under it.

options: The Council of State and the Federal Assembly
mcqs.why: The Act created a federal legislature of two houses — the Council of State and the Federal Assembly — under the Governor-General.

options: Defence, foreign affairs, communications and currency
mcqs.why: The federation retained defence, foreign affairs, communications, imports and exports, and currency, while other matters went to the autonomous provinces.

mcqs.q: When was Sindh separated from Bombay as a province under the Act?
mcqs.why: Sindh's separation, agreed at the Round Table Conferences and included in the 1935 Act, took effect in 1936, making Sindh a separate province.

mcqs.q: What share of the central legislature did the 1935 Act grant Muslims?
mcqs.why: The Government of India Act 1935 granted Muslims one-third representation in the central legislature and maintained separate electorates.

mcqs.why: The Act established a Federal Court at the centre as part of the federal scheme for India.

mcqs.why: Burma was separated from India under the Government of India Act 1935, one of the Act's ten important points listed in the book.

mcqs.why: The provincial part of the Act came into force on April 1, 1937, and provincial elections were held under it; the federal part was never implemented.

lessons.title: The 1937 Elections and the Congress Ministries
lessons.notes_html:
The 1937 elections were held under the provincial part of the Government of India Act 1935. Out of the 1,771 provincial seats, the Congress won 706 — less than half, proving it was not the representative party of all Indians. In Punjab the Unionist Party secured the majority and Sir Sikandar Hayat formed the ministry; in Bengal, A. K. Fazlul Huq of the Krishak Praja Party formed the ministry; and in Sindh, Sir Ghulam Hussain Hidayatullah formed the ministry. The Muslim League won 102 out of the 482 seats reserved for Muslims. The Congress formed ministries in seven provinces: U.P., C.P., Bihar, Bombay, Madras, Orissa and the North-West Frontier Province.

The Pirpur Report

The Congress ministries (1937–39) implemented anti-Muslim policies. On March 20, 1938, the Muslim League Council formed a committee of eight members headed by Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur, which visited six Congress-ruled provinces and on November 15, 1938 presented its report, 'Oppression of Muslims under Congress Rule' — the Pirpur Report. It recorded Congress interference in administration; the imposition of 'Vande Mataram' as the national anthem (written by Bankim Chandra Chatterji, from a novel in which Muslim rulers were depicted as robbers and looters); the hoisting of the Congress tricolour on government buildings; interference in Muslim religious practices such as beating drums before mosques, banning the Azan in some places and restrictions on cow slaughter; and the declaration of Hindi as the official language in various provinces. The report exposed Congress rule and strengthened the Muslim case.

mcqs.why: In the 1937 elections Congress won seven provinces — U.P., C.P., Bihar, Bombay, Madras, Orissa and the North-West Frontier Province — and formed ministries there.

mcqs.q: How many of the 482 Muslim-reserved seats did the Muslim League win in 1937?
mcqs.why: The Muslim League won 102 out of the 482 seats reserved for Muslims in the 1937 elections — a disappointing result that pushed Jinnah to reorganise the party.

mcqs.q: Out of 1,771 provincial seats, the Congress won:
mcqs.why: Congress won 706 of the 1,771 provincial seats — less than half — proving it was not the representative party of all Indians, as the book emphasises.

mcqs.q: Who formed the ministry in Punjab after the 1937 elections?
options: Sir Sikandar Hayat of the Unionist Party
mcqs.why: In Punjab the Unionist Party secured the majority and Sir Sikandar Hayat formed the ministry; the League failed to form a ministry in any province.

mcqs.q: Who formed the ministry in Bengal in 1937?
options: A. K. Fazlul Huq of the Krishak Praja Party
mcqs.why: In Bengal, A. K. Fazlul Huq of the Krishak Praja Party formed the ministry after the 1937 elections.

mcqs.q: The Pirpur Report was presented on:
mcqs.why: The Pirpur Committee presented its report, 'Oppression of Muslims under Congress Rule', on November 15, 1938, after visiting six Congress-ruled provinces.

mcqs.q: Who headed the committee that produced the Pirpur Report?
options: Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur
mcqs.why: The eight-member committee was headed by Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur, formed by the Muslim League Council on March 20, 1938.

mcqs.q: The anthem 'Vande Mataram' was written by:
mcqs.why: Vande Mataram was written by Bankim Chandra Chatterji and taken from his novel in which Muslim rulers were depicted as robbers and looters — a key Pirpur Report complaint.

mcqs.q: Which of these was recorded in the Pirpur Report?
options: Banning of the Azan in some places and drums beaten before mosques
mcqs.why: The Pirpur Report recorded interference in Muslim religious practices, such as beating drums in front of mosques, banning the Azan in some places and restrictions on cow slaughter.

mcqs.q: What was the twofold significance of the 1937 elections?
options: The League's weak result, but Congress's anti-Muslim rule convinced Muslims they needed a separate homeland
mcqs.why: The elections disappointed the League, but the anti-Muslim policies of the Congress ministries (1937–39) convinced Muslims of the need for a separate homeland and led Jinnah to reorganise the League.

lessons.title: Jinnah Reorganizes the Muslim League
lessons.notes_html:
After the failure of the Khilafat Movement, Hindu-Muslim unity was shattered, communal organisations like the Shuddhi and Sanghatan movements caused widespread riots, and the Muslim League was a very weak organisation, further divided over the Simon Commission and the Nehru Report. Muhammad Ali Jinnah first tried to reconcile the League's factions through his Fourteen Points.

Although the 1937 election results were not encouraging, between 1937 and 1939, during the Congress ministries, Jinnah successfully reorganised the Muslim League. Capitalising on the Congress's political blunders, he expanded the League's organisation in villages, towns, districts and provinces, formed student organisations, mobilised religious scholars, and strengthened the working committee's control in all provinces. Through statements and public meetings the League clearly articulated its demands, and its leaders toured the length and breadth of India to spread the demand for Pakistan. Quaid-e-Azam's slogan of Unity, Faith and Discipline became a living reality; League membership rose from 112,000 in 1941 to 2 million by 1944, and the British government began to recognise the Muslim League as the sole representative party of the Muslims of India.

Day of Deliverance

When the Second World War began, the Congress ministries resigned on October 31, 1939, dissatisfied with the Governor-General's declaration of war. Since Muslims had suffered oppression under the Congress ministries, Jinnah appealed to all Muslims to observe Yum-e-Najat (Day of Deliverance) on December 22, 1939, with thanksgiving prayers. Other minorities, including Christians, Parsis and Untouchables, also participated.

options: Unity had shattered after Khilafat and the League was divided over the Simon Commission and Nehru Report
It had no leader at all
mcqs.why: After Khilafat's failure, Hindu-Muslim unity shattered, communal riots spread, and the League was weak and divided over the Simon Commission and the Nehru Report.

mcqs.why: Jinnah first tried to reconcile the Muslim League's factions through his Fourteen Points of 1929, a common minimum programme for Muslims.

mcqs.why: Between 1937 and 1939, during the Congress ministries, Jinnah reorganised the League, capitalising on Congress's political blunders and anti-Muslim policies.

options: Students and religious scholars, with organisation down to village level
mcqs.why: Jinnah expanded the League in villages, towns, districts and provinces, formed student organisations and mobilised religious scholars behind the Pakistan demand.

mcqs.q: What was Quaid-e-Azam's famous slogan?
mcqs.why: Quaid-e-Azam's slogan of Unity, Faith and Discipline became a living reality as the reorganised League united Muslims behind him.

mcqs.why: Muslim League membership rose from 112,000 in 1941 to 2 million by 1944, and the British recognised it as the sole representative party of Indian Muslims.

mcqs.q: When did the Congress ministries resign?
mcqs.why: All Congress provincial ministries resigned on October 31, 1939, dissatisfied with the Governor-General's declaration that India would support the war.

mcqs.q: When was Yum-e-Najat (Day of Deliverance) observed?
mcqs.why: Jinnah appealed to Muslims to observe Yum-e-Najat (Day of Deliverance) on December 22, 1939, after the oppressive Congress ministries resigned.

mcqs.q: Why did Muslims celebrate the Day of Deliverance?
options: They had suffered oppression under the Congress ministries, whose rule had ended
mcqs.why: Muslims had suffered oppression under the Congress ministries (1937–1939), so the end of those ministries brought them joy and thanksgiving.

mcqs.q: Which other communities also participated in the Day of Deliverance?
mcqs.why: Other minorities, including Christians, Parsis and Untouchables, also participated in the Day of Deliverance, having suffered under Congress rule too.

chapters.title: Unit 7: World War-II and its Consequences (1939-45)

lessons.title: Causes of the Second World War
lessons.notes_html:
The book lists these main causes of the Second World War:

(1) The Treaty of Versailles: after World War-I the treaty occupied many German areas, crushed Germany's military power, imposed heavy reparations and humiliated Germany in every possible way, so feelings of revenge rose among the Germans; Hitler's Nazi Party aimed to abolish the treaty, restore Germany as a superpower and conquer all of Europe.

(2) Military alliances: in 1936 Hitler allied with Mussolini's Italy, Japan joined in 1937 to form the Axis Powers, and in 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a ten-year non-aggression pact whose secret clause divided Eastern Europe between them.

(3) Ideological division: the world was divided between democracy (Britain, France, the USA), dictatorship (Italy, Germany, Japan) and communism (the Soviet Union), which clashed with each other. (4) Failure of the League of Nations: it failed to intervene when Japan invaded Manchuria and Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, and was completely ineffective. (5) Appeasement: weak Britain and France appeased Germany, believing it had legitimate grievances and that a strong Germany would block communism; their silence over the occupation of Czechoslovakia in March 1939 encouraged Hitler. (6) The immediate cause: Germany's attack on Poland on September 1, 1939.

mcqs.q: When did the Second World War begin?
mcqs.why: The Second World War began in 1939, when Germany attacked Poland on September 1, 1939 — the war's immediate cause.

mcqs.q: What was the immediate cause of the Second World War?
options: Germany's attack on Poland on September 1, 1939
mcqs.why: The immediate cause was Germany's attack on Poland on September 1, 1939, after years of tension caused by Versailles, alliances and appeasement.

mcqs.q: How did the Treaty of Versailles help cause the Second World War?
options: It humiliated Germany and created feelings of revenge
mcqs.why: Versailles occupied German areas, crushed its military power, imposed heavy reparations and humiliated Germany, creating the revenge feelings Hitler exploited.

mcqs.q: Which countries formed the Axis Powers?
mcqs.why: In 1936 Hitler allied with Mussolini's Italy and Japan joined in 1937, forming the Axis Powers of Germany, Italy and Japan.

mcqs.q: In 1939, Germany signed a ten-year non-aggression pact with:
mcqs.why: In 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a ten-year non-aggression pact whose secret clause divided Eastern Europe between them.

mcqs.q: The world before 1939 was ideologically divided between:
mcqs.why: The book describes a three-way ideological division: democracy (Britain, France, USA), dictatorship (Italy, Germany, Japan) and communism (the Soviet Union).

mcqs.q: How did the League of Nations fail before the war?
options: It failed to act when Japan invaded Manchuria and Italy invaded Ethiopia
mcqs.why: The League failed to intervene when Japan invaded Manchuria and when Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, proving completely ineffective at stopping aggression.

mcqs.q: What was the policy of 'appeasement'?
options: Britain and France gave in to Germany, hoping a strong Germany would block communism
mcqs.why: Weak Britain and France appeased Germany, believing it had legitimate grievances and that a strong Germany would block communism — their silence over Czechoslovakia encouraged Hitler.

mcqs.q: Britain and France remained silent when Germany occupied which country in March 1939?
mcqs.why: Their silence over the occupation of Czechoslovakia in March 1939 encouraged Hitler to attack Poland six months later.

mcqs.q: What did Hitler's Nazi Party aim to do with the Treaty of Versailles?
options: Abolish it and restore Germany as a superpower
mcqs.why: Hitler's Nazi Party aimed to abolish the Treaty of Versailles, restore Germany as a superpower and conquer all of Europe.

lessons.title: Germany Attacks Russia and America Joins the War
lessons.notes_html:
Despite the ten-year non-aggression pact of 1939, Hitler's goals were not limited to the return of German territories; he aimed at the conquest of all of Europe. He therefore attacked Russia on June 22, 1941, without declaring war, and within four months Germany captured almost 50% of Russia's important coal, steel and iron-rich regions. However, heavy snowfall halted the German advance, and at Stalingrad the German forces were surrounded and forced to surrender.

Initially the United States remained neutral, but after Japan's air force attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the United States decided to join the Allied forces. Japan had also captured the Philippines, Singapore, Malaya and Burma, posing a threat to British India. America's involvement turned the tide of the war: US air and naval forces played a pivotal role, American transport aircraft continuously supplied the Allied forces with war materials, and US airstrikes on Germany were crucial in breaking down Germany's military power. Finally, after Japan refused to surrender, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and Japan surrendered in September 1945.

mcqs.q: When did Germany attack the Soviet Union?
mcqs.why: Germany attacked Russia on June 22, 1941, without declaring war, breaking the 1939 non-aggression pact.

mcqs.q: Why did Hitler attack Russia despite the non-aggression pact?
options: His aim was the conquest of all of Europe, not just German territories
mcqs.why: Hitler's goals were not limited to regaining German territories; he aimed at the conquest of all of Europe, so he attacked Russia in 1941.

mcqs.q: Within four months of the invasion, Germany had captured:
options: Almost 50% of Russia's coal, steel and iron-rich regions
mcqs.why: Within four months Germany captured almost 50% of Russia's important coal, steel and iron-rich regions, before snow and Stalingrad halted the advance.

mcqs.q: What halted the German advance in Russia?
options: Heavy snowfall and the defeat at Stalingrad
mcqs.why: Heavy snowfall halted the German advance, and at Stalingrad the German forces were surrounded and forced to surrender — a turning point of the war.

mcqs.q: When did the United States join the Second World War?
mcqs.why: The United States joined the war in 1941, after Japan's attack on the US naval base at Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

mcqs.q: Why did the United States join the war?
options: Germany declared war on it in 1939
Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor
mcqs.why: America remained neutral until Japan's air force attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941; it then joined the Allied forces.

mcqs.q: Which places had Japan captured, threatening British India?
options: The Philippines, Singapore, Malaya and Burma
mcqs.why: Japan had captured the Philippines, Singapore, Malaya (Indonesia) and Burma (Myanmar), posing a direct threat to British India.

mcqs.q: How did America's entry affect the war?
options: It turned the tide in favour of the Allies
mcqs.why: America's involvement turned the tide: US air and naval forces were pivotal, its transports supplied the Allies, and its airstrikes broke Germany's military power.

mcqs.q: On which Japanese cities did the United States drop atomic bombs?
mcqs.why: After Japan refused to surrender, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and Japan surrendered in September 1945.

mcqs.q: At which Russian city were German forces surrounded and forced to surrender?
mcqs.why: At Stalingrad the German forces were surrounded and forced to surrender, after heavy snowfall had already halted their advance into Russia.

lessons.title: Germany's Defeat and the Results of the War
lessons.notes_html:
Germany was defeated because: its attack on Russia failed — heavy snowfall halted its advance and its forces surrendered at Stalingrad; the United States joined the Allies in 1941 and turned the tide, supplying war materials and breaking Germany's military power through airstrikes; its ally Italy surrendered to the Allies in 1944; and Britain, left to fight alone in 1940, survived the German airstrikes. On May 8, 1945, Germany accepted defeat and the war in Europe ended.

Outcomes of the war

The war caused massive destruction worldwide: around 30 million people were killed, half of them from Russia, and 21 million were left homeless; it led to famine and the spread of diseases, and Germany was completely destroyed. The United States emerged as a superpower. Immediately after the war, tensions between the United States and the Soviet Union escalated into the Cold War (1945–1990). The United Nations was established in 1945 to prevent a third world war. For India, the war began the decline of the British Empire: by 1945 Britain's position had weakened so much that maintaining control over India was no longer possible, and the results of the 1945–46 elections paved the way for the creation of Pakistan.

mcqs.q: When did Germany accept defeat, ending the war in Europe?
mcqs.why: On May 8, 1945, Germany accepted defeat and the war in Europe ended, after the failures in Russia and the Allied onslaught.

mcqs.q: Which of Germany's allies surrendered to the Allies in 1944?
mcqs.why: Germany's ally Italy surrendered to the Allies in 1944, further weakening the Axis position in Europe.

mcqs.q: Approximately how many people were killed in the Second World War?
mcqs.why: Around 30 million people were killed in the Second World War, half of them from Russia, and 21 million were left homeless.

mcqs.q: Half of the war's 30 million dead were from which country?
mcqs.why: Half of the approximately 30 million people killed in the war were from Russia, which bore the heaviest human cost of the conflict.

mcqs.q: How many people were left homeless by the war?
mcqs.why: The war left 21 million people homeless and caused famine and disease on a massive scale; Germany itself was completely destroyed.

mcqs.q: Which country emerged from the war as a superpower?
mcqs.why: The United States rose to prominence, helped the Allies achieve victory and emerged from the war as a superpower.

mcqs.q: What began between the USA and the USSR immediately after the war?
mcqs.why: Immediately after the war, tensions between the United States and the Soviet Union escalated into the Cold War, which lasted from 1945 to 1990.

options: To prevent a third world war
mcqs.why: The United Nations was established in 1945 to prevent a third world war and maintain international peace and security.

mcqs.q: What did the war mean for British rule in India?
options: Britain weakened so much that holding India was no longer possible
mcqs.why: By 1945 Britain's position had weakened so much that maintaining control over India was no longer possible; the 1945–46 elections paved the way for Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Which factor did NOT contribute to Germany's defeat, according to the book?
options: Failure of the attack on Russia
mcqs.why: Germany's defeat came from the failed Russian campaign, America's entry, Italy's surrender and Britain's survival — Japan never conquered Britain.

lessons.title: The United Nations
lessons.notes_html:
The objectives of the United Nations, outlined in Article 1 of its Charter, are: (1) to maintain international peace and security; (2) to put an end to all forms of aggression; (3) to settle international disputes peacefully and in accordance with international law; (4) to promote friendly relations between nations; (5) to foster international cooperation; and (6) to protect fundamental human rights. Its six main organs are the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, the Secretariat and the International Court of Justice.

The Security Council

The Security Council is the most powerful organ of the United Nations. It has 15 members: 5 permanent (the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, France and the People's Republic of China), who have veto power, and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms by the General Assembly. Decisions require a majority of nine votes, which must include the votes of the five permanent members; a negative vote by any permanent member is a veto. The Council maintains international peace and security by investigating disputes, imposing sanctions and authorising peacekeeping or military actions.

mcqs.q: In which year was the United Nations established?
mcqs.why: The United Nations was established in 1945, after the Second World War, to prevent another world war.

mcqs.q: The objectives of the United Nations are outlined in which part of its Charter?
mcqs.why: The UN's objectives — peace and security, ending aggression, peaceful settlement of disputes, friendly relations, cooperation and human rights — are outlined in Article 1 of its Charter.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the six main organs of the United Nations?
mcqs.why: The six main organs are the General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, Trusteeship Council, Secretariat and International Court of Justice; the League of Nations was the UN's predecessor.

mcqs.q: How many members does the UN Security Council have?
mcqs.why: The Security Council has 15 members: 5 permanent members with veto power and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.

mcqs.q: Which countries are the five permanent members of the Security Council?
options: Russia, China, India, Pakistan and Egypt
USA, UK, Russia, France and China
USA, Germany, Japan, India and Brazil
UK, France, Italy, Spain and Canada
mcqs.why: The five permanent members are the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, France and the People's Republic of China.

options: Double votes in the General Assembly
mcqs.why: Each permanent member holds veto power: a negative vote by any one of them blocks a Security Council decision.

mcqs.why: The 10 non-permanent members of the Security Council are elected for two-year terms by the General Assembly.

options: A majority of nine, including the five permanent members
mcqs.why: Decisions require a majority of nine votes, which must include the votes of the five permanent members — hence the importance of the veto.

mcqs.q: How does the Security Council maintain peace and security?
options: By investigating disputes, imposing sanctions and authorising peacekeeping or military action
mcqs.why: The Council maintains international peace and security by investigating disputes, imposing sanctions and authorising peacekeeping or military actions.

mcqs.q: One objective of the United Nations is to:
options: Create a world army under one nation
mcqs.why: Article 1 of the UN Charter includes putting an end to all forms of aggression and settling disputes peacefully under international law.

lessons.title: The Cold War and the Palestine Issue
lessons.notes_html:
The Cold War was a state of tension between the United States and the Soviet Union that lasted from 1945 to 1990, characterised by an arms race, military alliances, propaganda, espionage, military coups and interventions in Asia, Africa and Latin America, without a direct war between the two. Its main cause was the ideological conflict between communism and capitalism. Its effects on Pakistan were: Pakistan joined the US-backed alliances CENTO (1955) and SEATO (1955) to strengthen its defence capability and economy, and when the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in 1979, Pakistan had to bear the burden of over 3 million Afghan refugees, along with serious social and economic issues.

Palestine and Israel

Before World War-I, people of all three religions lived in peace in Palestine, and Jews, spread across the world, longed for a homeland there. In the 1880s, Jews from Russia and Eastern Europe began settling in Palestine with the aid of international Jewish capitalists. In 1897 the first World Jewish Congress at Basel (Switzerland) resolved to establish a Jewish state in Palestine, and the International Zionist Movement was established. On November 2, 1917, British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour issued the Balfour Declaration, supporting a 'national home' for the Jewish people in Palestine, although Jews then made up only 5% of its population. After World War-I the League of Nations gave Britain the mandate over Palestine and Jewish immigration increased. In November 1947 the UN General Assembly proposed the partition of Palestine into an Arab state and a Jewish state (Israel), with international control over Jerusalem; the Arabs rejected it, but in 1948 Israel was established; the Arab nations attacked and were defeated, and millions of Palestinians were displaced.

mcqs.why: The book's timeline places the beginning of the Cold War in 1945, and its text dates the Cold War from 1945 to 1990.

options: The United States and the Soviet Union
mcqs.why: The Cold War (1945–1990) was the tension between the United States and the Soviet Union, fought through arms races, alliances and propaganda rather than direct war.

mcqs.q: What was the main cause of the Cold War?
options: The ideological conflict between communism and capitalism
mcqs.why: The main cause of the Cold War was the ideological conflict between communism, championed by the USSR, and capitalism, championed by the USA.

mcqs.q: Which US-backed alliances did Pakistan join in 1955?
mcqs.why: Pakistan joined the US-backed alliances CENTO (1955) and SEATO (1955) to strengthen its defence capability and economy during the Cold War.

mcqs.q: When the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in 1979, Pakistan had to bear the burden of:
mcqs.why: Pakistan bore the burden of over 3 million Afghan refugees after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, with serious social and economic effects.

mcqs.q: When was the Balfour Declaration issued?
mcqs.why: British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour issued the Balfour Declaration on November 2, 1917, supporting a 'national home' for the Jewish people in Palestine.

mcqs.q: What did the Balfour Declaration support?
options: A 'national home' for the Jewish people in Palestine
mcqs.why: The Balfour Declaration supported a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, although Jews then made up only 5% of its population.

mcqs.q: The first World Jewish Congress at Basel resolved in 1897 to:
options: Establish a Jewish state in Palestine
mcqs.why: The first World Jewish Congress at Basel (Switzerland) in 1897 resolved to establish a Jewish state in Palestine, and the International Zionist Movement was established.

mcqs.why: In November 1947 the UN proposed partitioning Palestine into an Arab state and a Jewish state (Israel) with international control over Jerusalem; the Arabs rejected the plan.

mcqs.why: Israel was established in 1948 after the UN partition proposal; the Arab nations attacked and were defeated, and millions of Palestinians were displaced.

lessons.title: The Lahore Resolution 1940
lessons.notes_html:
The Lahore Resolution was passed on March 23, 1940, at the Lahore session of the Muslim League. It was presented by A. K. Fazlul Haq, the Chief Minister of Bengal, after Quaid-e-Azam's presidential address. The Resolution declared that no constitutional plan would be workable unless based on these principles:

(1) The geographically contiguous units should be demarcated into regions such that the areas where Muslims are in a majority, such as the North-Western and Eastern zones, should be grouped to constitute 'independent states' in which the constituent units shall be autonomous and sovereign, and the constitution shall provide adequate, effective and mandatory safeguards for minorities' economic, cultural, political, administrative and other rights.

(2) In areas where Muslims are in a minority, adequate, effective and mandatory safeguards should be provided for the protection of their religious, cultural, economic, political, administrative and other rights.

(3) The Muslim League Working Committee was authorised to draft a constitutional scheme granting the concerned regions full powers such as defence, foreign affairs, communications and taxation.

mcqs.q: Who presented the Lahore Resolution?
mcqs.why: The Lahore Resolution was presented by A. K. Fazlul Haq, the Chief Minister of Bengal, at the Lahore session of March 23, 1940, after Quaid-e-Azam's presidential address.

mcqs.q: When was the Lahore Resolution passed?
mcqs.why: The Lahore Resolution was passed on March 23, 1940, at Lahore — the day now celebrated as Pakistan Day.

mcqs.q: The Lahore Resolution demanded that Muslim-majority areas in the North-Western and Eastern zones be grouped to form:
mcqs.why: The Resolution demanded that Muslim-majority areas of the North-Western and Eastern zones be grouped to constitute independent states with autonomous and sovereign units.

options: Adequate, effective and mandatory safeguards for their rights
mcqs.why: The Resolution required the constitution to provide adequate, effective and mandatory safeguards for minorities' economic, cultural, political, administrative and other rights.

mcqs.q: For Muslims living in minority areas, the Resolution demanded:
options: Adequate safeguards for their religious, cultural, economic and political rights
mcqs.why: In areas where Muslims were in a minority, the Resolution demanded adequate, effective and mandatory safeguards for their religious, cultural, economic, political and other rights.

mcqs.q: Who was authorised by the Resolution to draft a constitutional scheme?
mcqs.why: The Muslim League Working Committee was authorised to draft a constitutional scheme granting the regions full powers such as defence, foreign affairs, communications and taxation.

options: Defence, foreign affairs, communications and taxation
mcqs.why: The scheme was to grant the concerned regions full powers such as defence, foreign affairs, communications and taxation — the marks of sovereign states.

mcqs.q: A. K. Fazlul Haq, who moved the Resolution, was Chief Minister of:
mcqs.why: A. K. Fazlul Haq was the Chief Minister of Bengal; he had earlier formed the Bengal ministry after the 1937 elections.

mcqs.why: The Resolution was passed at the Lahore session of the All India Muslim League in March 1940, presided over by Quaid-e-Azam.

mcqs.why: The Resolution stated that the independent states would have constituent units that were autonomous and sovereign.

lessons.title: The Cripps Mission and the Quit India Movement
lessons.notes_html:
Sir Stafford Cripps arrived in India on March 20, 1942, with proposals from the British government. The Muslim League was satisfied that the Cripps proposals acknowledged its demand for the division of India, since one clause, allowing provinces to separate, provided a possible path for the creation of Pakistan. However, the League rejected the proposals because their primary aim was to establish a united Indian union; the formation of multiple unions and the possibility of separation of provinces were unclear, which made the prospect of a separate Muslim homeland uncertain and difficult. According to the Lahore Resolution, the League had already declared the partition of India as the only constitutional solution.

The Congress also rejected the Cripps proposals. In 1942 the Second World War was knocking at India's door and Britain's position had weakened. Taking advantage of the wartime situation, the Congress launched the Quit India Movement on August 8, 1942, aiming to pressure the British government, trapped in war, to end British rule in India, and also to send a message to the Muslim League to withdraw its demand for a separate homeland. The British crushed the movement with an iron hand and arrested the Congress leaders.

lessons.title: Direct Action Day
lessons.notes_html:
After the Cabinet Mission Plan failed, the Governor-General invited the Congress to form the government instead of the Muslim League, which had accepted the plan. In response, Jinnah withdrew his agreement to join the interim government, and the Muslim League Council declared 16 August 1946 as Direct Action Day, calling upon Muslims across India to peacefully protest against the government's betrayal.

Unfortunately, under the incitement of the Congress and Hindu extremists (as the book states), the day turned into violent Hindu-Muslim riots in Calcutta, Noakhali and Bihar, among the worst in India's history, resulting in thousands of deaths and widespread destruction, and the army had to be deployed. The tragedy convinced all sides that Hindus and Muslims could no longer live together in one state, hastening the partition of India.

lessons.title: The Indian Independence Act and the Creation of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
The British government passed the Indian Independence Act on 18 July 1947. Its main points were: (1) from 15 August 1947, British India would become independent, resulting in the creation of two sovereign states, Pakistan and India; (2) all governing powers were transferred to these two states and British rule officially ended; (3) British control over the Indian princely states also ended, all treaties between them and the British Crown were annulled, and the princely states were free to accede to either India or Pakistan; (4) two separate Constituent Assemblies were provided, each with the power to legislate and frame its own constitution; (5) until new constitutions were framed, both governments would operate under the Government of India Act 1935 with amendments, and each Constituent Assembly would serve as the central legislature during the transition; and (6) the Governor General would supervise the division of armed forces and assets between the two countries.

Under this Act, Pakistan officially came into being on 14 August 1947.

mcqs.why: The Indian Independence Act was passed on 18 July 1947, providing for two sovereign states, Pakistan and India, from 15 August 1947.

mcqs.why: The Act created two sovereign states, Pakistan and India, and all governing powers were transferred to them as British rule officially ended.

mcqs.why: Two separate Constituent Assemblies were provided, each with power to legislate and frame its own constitution, also serving as the central legislature during the transition.

options: The Government of India Act 1935, with amendments
mcqs.why: Until new constitutions were framed, both governments operated under the Government of India Act 1935 with amendments.

mcqs.why: Under the Act, the Governor General would supervise the division of armed forces and assets between Pakistan and India.

mcqs.why: The Act transferred all governing powers to Pakistan and India, and British rule over India officially ended.

mcqs.why: The book's timeline lists the 3rd June Plan for Partition in 1947, followed by the Indian Independence Act of 18 July 1947 and the creation of Pakistan.

lessons.title: Quaid-e-Azam, Students and Women in the Pakistan Movement
lessons.notes_html:
Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah's role was decisive at every stage. He entered politics in 1906, joined the Muslim League in 1913, and played a pivotal role in the Lucknow Pact of 1916. Disillusioned by the Nehru Report and the Round Table Conferences, he withdrew to Britain, returned in 1934 and reorganised the divided Muslim League. He led the adoption of the Lahore Resolution on 23 March 1940, rejected the Wavell Plan in 1945, declared the League the sole representative of Indian Muslims in the 1945 elections, accepted the Cabinet Mission Plan in 1946 but rejected it after British betrayal, and called Direct Action Day. Through his inspiring leadership and strategic political acumen, Pakistan came into existence on 14 August 1947.

Students

Muslim students acted as Jinnah's vanguard. In 1935 the Aligarh Muslim Students' Federation was established with his support; the All India Muslim Students Federation followed, its first session held on December 27, 1937, in Calcutta, presided over by Jinnah. Qazi Isa founded the Balochistan Muslim Students Federation in 1943, and students campaigned actively in the 1945–46 elections and the 1947 NWFP referendum.

Women

Jinnah wanted Muslim women to participate in politics alongside men. In 1938 he established the Women's Wing of the League in Patna. Prominent women included Miss Fatima Jinnah, Begum Mohammad Ali Jouhar, Begum Ra'ana Liaquat Ali Khan and Begum Shaista Ikramullah. Begum Mohammad Ali Jouhar was the first Muslim woman to be imprisoned during the freedom struggle. Women campaigned actively in the 1946 elections and, after 1947, played a critical role in refugee rehabilitation.

mcqs.why: Disillusioned by the Nehru Report and the Round Table Conferences, Jinnah withdrew to Britain, returned in 1934 and reorganised the divided Muslim League.

mcqs.why: In 1945 Jinnah rejected the Wavell Plan, then declared the League the sole representative of Indian Muslims for the 1945 elections.

mcqs.why: In 1935, with Jinnah's support, the Aligarh Muslim Students' Federation was established, and similar organisations emerged in Punjab and Bengal.

mcqs.why: The first session of the All India Muslim Students Federation was held on December 27, 1937, in Calcutta, presided over by Jinnah.

mcqs.why: After 1947 the women of the movement played a critical role in refugee rehabilitation, helping resettle the millions who migrated to Pakistan.

lessons.title: Migration and the Radcliffe Award
lessons.notes_html:
A Boundary Commission under Sir Cyril Radcliffe was established on June 30, 1947, for the partition of Bengal and Punjab, but Viceroy Lord Mountbatten put considerable pressure on it. As a result of the Radcliffe Award: key Muslim-majority areas in Eastern Punjab, such as Gurdaspur, Batala and parts of Pathankot, were included in India, granting India road access to Jammu and Kashmir and facilitating its occupation of the region; and Muslim-majority tehsils in Amritsar, Jalandhar and Ferozepur, which controlled the headworks of irrigation canals, were also included in India. The award placed the canal headworks of the Ravi and Sutlej rivers under Indian control.

Even before the announcement of partition, Hindu-Muslim riots had begun, and with the announcement, extremist Hindus and Sikhs launched an organised massacre of Muslims in Delhi, Eastern Punjab, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, forcing Muslims to migrate to Pakistan for safety. It became the largest migration in human history: over seven million Muslims migrated to Pakistan, about 5.5 million Hindus and Sikhs migrated from West Pakistan to India, a total of fifteen million people were displaced and more than one million were killed. The consequences for Pakistan were a huge refugee and resettlement problem: the government established a Ministry for Refugees, Quaid-e-Azam visited refugee camps on September 1, 1947, and set up a relief fund, and committees and volunteer organisations assisted in resettling the displaced.

lessons.title: The Kashmir Issue
lessons.notes_html:
The book gives three reasons for the Kashmir issue: (1) Kashmir was a Muslim-majority state (77% Muslim according to the 1941 census) which should naturally have joined Pakistan, but its Hindu ruler, Maharaja Hari Singh, was reluctant to do so; (2) India's Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, himself a Kashmiri Pandit, opposed Kashmir joining Pakistan, and Mountbatten, Nehru and Gandhi exerted pressure on the Maharaja to accede to India; and (3) the Radcliffe Award gave India the Muslim-majority areas of Gurdaspur, Batala and Pathankot, granting India road access to Jammu and Kashmir, which facilitated its occupation of the region.

The Maharaja's use of force against Kashmiri Muslims protesting in favour of Pakistan turned the dispute into a war. Indian troops entered Kashmir on October 27, 1947. The United Nations passed resolutions on Kashmir — the book dates the UN resolution calling for a plebiscite in Kashmir to April 21, 1948, and a later resolution to August 13, 1948; a ceasefire was announced at the end of December 1948. The promised plebiscite has never been held.

lessons.title: The Objectives Resolution and the 1956 Constitution
lessons.notes_html:
The Objectives Resolution was passed on March 12, 1949. Its important points were: (1) sovereignty belongs solely to Allah alone; (2) the power to govern is a sacred trust, and the elected representatives of the people will exercise this power; and (3) democracy, freedom, equality, tolerance, justice and the principles of governance, as defined by Islam, will be followed. It also provided that Muslims would be enabled to practise Islam according to the Quran and Sunnah, the rights and culture of minorities would be respected and protected, Pakistan would be a federation with autonomous provinces, basic human rights would be guaranteed, and the judiciary would be independent.

The 1956 Constitution

The first constitution was enforced on March 23, 1956, and Iskander Mirza became the first President. Its features: the country was named the 'Islamic Republic of Pakistan', no law could contradict Islamic laws, the President was required to be a Muslim, and the Objectives Resolution was included as the preamble; it was a federal constitution of West and East Pakistan with equal status; a parliamentary system in which the Prime Minister and cabinet were accountable to the National Assembly; a unicameral National Assembly of 300 members, 150 from each wing, with ten seats reserved for women; an independent judiciary; fundamental rights for all citizens; and Urdu and Bengali as official languages, with English to remain official for 25 years.

It failed because it was never fully implemented, promised elections were never held, and after the deaths of Quaid-e-Azam (September 11, 1948) and Liaquat Ali Khan (assassinated 1951), weak leadership and conspiracies replaced four Prime Ministers between 1956 and 1958. On October 7, 1958, Iskander Mirza imposed martial law, the constitution was suspended, and General Ayub Khan took control.

lessons.title: Ayub Khan's Era of Development
lessons.notes_html:
Ayub Khan's era (October 27, 1958 – March 25, 1969) is considered a golden period of economic development, often called the 'decade of development'. Agrarian reforms (January 24, 1959) fixed a ceiling of 500 acres of irrigated or 1,000 acres of rain-fed land, distributed excess land among farmers and protected tenants; the Green Revolution provided farmers with loans and seeds on easy terms, fertiliser factories were established, modern agricultural machinery was introduced, and salinity and waterlogging were addressed, making Pakistan self-sufficient in grain. Industrial reforms encouraged private investors through tax exemptions and loans.

From November 1, 1959, Ayub Khan introduced the Basic Democracies system, whose tiers were: (a) Union Council; (b) Tehsil Council; (c) District Council; (d) Divisional Council; and (e) Provincial Advisory Council. Its 120,000 members (60,000 from each wing) resolved local issues and voted in elections for the assemblies and the President.

The Indus Water Treaty (September 19, 1960) led to the Indus Basin Project, including Mangla Dam on the Jhelum (completed 1967), Tarbela Dam on the Indus, five barrages and interconnecting canals. Other milestones included the Warsak Dam (1961), the Guddu Barrage (1963), television stations at Lahore (1964), the Atomic Energy Commission (1965), the completion of the new capital Islamabad (1966) and housing for refugees at Korangi Colony (1960). The RCD (1964) with Iran and Turkey brought further industrial progress.

lessons.title: The Wars of 1965 and 1971
lessons.notes_html:
In May 1965 Indian forces captured some posts in the Rann of Kutch but were forced to retreat by swift Pakistani action, and the war extended to the Lahore, Sialkot, Khem Karan and Rajasthan sectors. At Lahore, a Pakistani company halted the Indian advance at the BRB Canal; Major Aziz Bhatti was martyred on the night of September 9–10, 1965, defending Lahore, and was awarded the Nishan-e-Haider. At Chawinda (Sialkot), India attacked with 600 tanks; in the largest tank battle after World War II, 150 Indian tanks were destroyed. Pakistani forces captured Khem Karan on September 11 and the Mona Bao railway station in Rajasthan on September 13. The Pakistan Navy attacked the port of Dwarka on the night of September 7–8, and the Pakistan Air Force's Squadron Leader M. M. Alam shot down five Indian aircraft in five minutes on September 7 — a world record. The UN Security Council called for a ceasefire on September 20; the war ended on September 23, 1965, and under the Soviet-mediated Tashkent Agreement (January 10, 1966) both forces returned to the international borders.

The 1971 War

The book gives these reasons: India never fully accepted Pakistan's existence and had illegally occupied Kashmir; after 1965 India changed strategy to focus on separating East Pakistan, encouraging separatist sentiments and training the 'Mukti Bahini'; and the political crisis after Pakistan's first general elections (December 1970), in which the Awami League won 167 National Assembly seats and the PPP 86, ended in deadlock — Sheikh Mujibur Rahman demanded transfer of power, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto wanted power-sharing, and Mujib refused any compromise. On December 3, 1971, India attacked Western Pakistan. East Pakistan was separated, and the independence of Bangladesh was officially declared on December 21, 1971 (as printed in the book).

lessons.title: The Afghan War and the War on Terror
lessons.notes_html:
The Afghan war grew out of the Cold War rivalry. In 1978, Nur Muhammad Taraki of the People's Democratic Party led the Saur Revolution, overthrew President Daoud Khan and established a pro-Soviet regime; Hafizullah Amin then seized power in 1979. After the Iranian Revolution of 1979, the United States, having lost its ally the Shah of Iran, leaned towards Amin. To counter US influence, Soviet troops entered Kabul on December 27, 1979, killed President Hafizullah Amin and installed Babrak Karmal, marking the beginning of the Afghan War.

Effects on Pakistan: millions of Afghan civilians sought refuge in Pakistan — by 2001 their number had reached around 4 million — and Pakistan bore this burden for decades; the war also brought militancy and terrorism to Pakistan's tribal areas. The Soviet Union withdrew in 1989 under the Geneva Accord; civil war followed among the Mujahideen groups, and the Taliban emerged in Kandahar in 1995.

The War on Terror

After the 9/11 attacks of September 11, 2001, the United States held Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda responsible, invaded Afghanistan and labelled the war the War on Terror; the Taliban government was overthrown in November 2001. The impacts on Pakistan were severe: over 80,000 Pakistanis lost their lives in terrorist incidents; Pakistan's economy suffered a loss exceeding $123 billion; and approximately 3.5 million civilians were displaced from the tribal areas. The Pakistan Army played a significant role: Operation 'Rah-e-Haq' cleared Swat in 2007, Operation 'Siraat-e-Mustaqeem' was conducted in Khyber Agency in 2008, and large-scale operations named 'Zarb-e-Azb' and 'Radd-ul-Fasad' were launched across the country (2014, as printed in the book). Pakistan also helped the peace process that led to the 2020 Doha deal.
